Ancient History.Prehistoric India:
INTRODUCTION
Prehistory refers to the period before the invention of writing. It is reconstructed through archaeological evidence such as stone tools, bones, plant remains, habitation sites and rock paintings. It represents the earliest stage of human cultural evolution and shows the gradual transition from food gathering to food production.

PALEOLITHIC AGE
The Paleolithic Age or Old Stone Age is the earliest phase of human history. It broadly extended from about 2.5 million years ago to around 10000 BCE. Human life was entirely dependent on nature and based on hunting, scavenging and food gathering.

FEATURES
• Stone tools formed the primary cultural evidence of this phase
• Tools were mainly made of quartzite using core and flake techniques
• Major tool types include hand axes, cleavers and choppers
• Human groups lived a nomadic life without permanent settlements
• Caves and rock shelters were used for temporary habitation
• Fire was known in later stages and used for cooking and protection
• No evidence of agriculture, pottery or domestication

The Paleolithic phase is divided into Lower, Middle and Upper stages based on tool development. The Lower Paleolithic is associated with Acheulian hand axe culture. The Middle Paleolithic shows dominance of flake tools. The Upper Paleolithic reflects blade tools, improved hunting and early artistic activity.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is known for rock shelters and early rock paintings
• Hunsgi in Karnataka shows habitation near raw material zones
• Kurnool caves in Andhra Pradesh indicate cave dwelling
• Belan Valley in Uttar Pradesh shows long cultural continuity
• Soan Valley in the north west is important for early tool traditions

MESOLITHIC AGE
The Mesolithic Age or Middle Stone Age represents a transitional phase between Paleolithic and Neolithic. It broadly dates from about 10000 BCE to 6000 BCE and developed after the end of the Ice Age.

FEATURES
• Microliths are the defining feature of this phase
• Small stone tools were often fitted into wood or bone to form composite tools
• Hunting and gathering continued but fishing and plant collection increased
• Semi sedentary settlements began to appear
• Early domestication of animals such as dog is seen
• Burials with grave goods indicate emerging belief systems

This phase represents adaptation to changing climate and environment rather than a complete break from the Paleolithic past.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bagor in Rajasthan provides evidence of animal domestication
• Langhnaj in Gujarat shows hunting and food gathering patterns
• Sarai Nahar Rai in Uttar Pradesh is known for burial practices
• Mahadaha is another important Mesolithic burial site
• Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh reflects microlithic continuity

NEOLITHIC AGE
The Neolithic Age or New Stone Age marks the beginning of food production. It appeared in different regions of India at different times from about 7000 BCE onward.

FEATURES
• Agriculture and animal domestication became the main economic activities
• Polished stone tools replaced earlier rough tools
• Permanent settlements and village life developed
• Pottery, weaving and storage of grains became common
• Use of grinding stones, pestles and sickles indicates cultivation
• Social organisation became more stable with settled communities

The Neolithic phase marks a shift from dependence on nature to control over resources and is often described as the Neolithic Revolution.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Mehrgarh is one of the earliest farming settlements with wheat and barley cultivation
• Mehrgarh also shows early evidence of dentistry and craft activity
• Burzahom in Kashmir is known for pit dwellings and burial practices
• Gufkral is another important Neolithic site in Kashmir
• Chirand in Bihar shows farming and settled life in eastern India
• Hallur and Maski indicate Neolithic expansion in South India

REGIONAL PATTERN
Neolithic culture developed differently across regions. In the north west, Mehrgarh shows early agriculture and domestication. In Kashmir, pit dwellings and burial practices are distinctive. In eastern India, Chirand reflects settled agriculture. In South India, cattle rearing, polished stone axes and ash mounds mark Neolithic culture.

SIGNIFICANCE
Prehistoric India reflects the long transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture and settled life. The development of food production led to surplus, population growth and stable communities. These changes laid the foundation for craft production, social differentiation and the emergence of early civilizations.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Paleolithic culture is identified by large stone tools and hunting gathering economy
• Mesolithic culture is identified by microliths and transitional subsistence
• Neolithic culture is identified by agriculture, domestication and polished tools
• Bhimbetka is important for rock art and continuous habitation
• Mehrgarh is crucial for earliest farming evidence in the subcontinent
• Burzahom is important for pit dwellings and factual questions

PYQ TRAP
Microliths belong to the Mesolithic phase. Agriculture and polished stone tools belong only to the Neolithic phase and not to the Paleolithic.
Ancient History.Indus Valley Civilization:
INTRODUCTION
The Indus Valley Civilization was one of the earliest urban civilizations of the world. It developed around 2500 BCE in the north western part of the Indian subcontinent. It is also known as the Harappan Civilization after the first discovered site. It was characterised by advanced urban planning, drainage systems and a high level of social organisation.

EXTENT
The civilization extended from Sutkagendor in Baluchistan to Alamgirpur in western Uttar Pradesh and from Manda in Jammu to Daimabad in Maharashtra. Major river systems included the Indus and its tributaries as well as the Ghaggar Hakra region.

TOWN PLANNING
• Cities were well planned with a grid pattern of streets
• Roads intersected at right angles showing advanced civic sense
• Division into citadel and lower town was a common feature
• Houses were built of burnt bricks with uniform proportions
• Most houses had access to wells and bathrooms

DRAINAGE SYSTEM
• One of the most remarkable features of the civilization
• Covered drains ran along streets and were connected to houses
• Drains had inspection holes for cleaning
• Indicates strong municipal authority and planning

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was the main occupation with crops like wheat and barley
• Evidence of rice cultivation at Lothal and Rangpur
• Use of plough is suggested by Kalibangan furrows
• Domestication of animals such as cattle, sheep and goat
• Craft production included bead making, pottery, metallurgy and textiles
• Cotton cultivation is one of the earliest in the world

TRADE
• Internal trade was well developed among different regions
• External trade with Mesopotamia is confirmed by seals and records
• Standardised weights and measures indicate regulated trade
• Lothal is considered an important port town with dockyard structure

SCRIPT
• The Harappan script is pictographic and remains undeciphered
• Found mainly on seals and pottery
• Short inscriptions suggest limited use for administrative purposes

RELIGION
• Evidence of worship of mother goddess indicating fertility cult
• Presence of proto Shiva figure in yogic posture on seals
• Worship of trees, animals and sacred symbols is indicated
• No clear evidence of temples or large scale religious structures

ART AND CULTURE
• Bronze sculpture of dancing girl from Mohenjo Daro shows artistic skill
• Bearded priest figure reflects possible elite class
• Terracotta figurines were common
• Pottery was well made and often decorated

IMPORTANT SITES
• Harappa in Punjab was the first discovered site
• Mohenjo Daro in Sindh is known for the Great Bath and granary
• Dholavira in Gujarat shows unique water management system
• Lothal in Gujarat is known for dockyard and trade
• Kalibangan in Rajasthan shows evidence of ploughed field
• Rakhigarhi in Haryana is one of the largest sites

DECLINE
The decline of the civilization occurred around 1900 BCE. Multiple factors are suggested.
• Environmental changes such as drying of rivers
• Floods in some regions
• Decline in trade networks
• Gradual shift towards rural settlements

SIGNIFICANCE
The Indus Valley Civilization represents the first urbanisation in the Indian subcontinent. It shows a high degree of planning, economic organisation and cultural development. Many features such as town planning and craft traditions influenced later cultures.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Use of burnt bricks and standardised weights is a key feature
• Drainage system is the most advanced feature
• Script remains undeciphered
• No clear evidence of monarchy or large temples
• Lothal is associated with maritime trade

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about urban features. Remember that drainage system, grid planning and standardised bricks are defining features, while large temples and palaces are not clearly evidenced.
Ancient History.Vedic Age:
INTRODUCTION
The Vedic Age marks the period of early Indo Aryan culture in the Indian subcontinent. It is known primarily from the Vedas, especially the Rigveda. It is broadly divided into Early Vedic and Later Vedic phases, reflecting significant social, economic and political changes.

EARLY VEDIC AGE
The Early Vedic period roughly spans from 1500 BCE to 1000 BCE. The Aryans initially settled in the north western region known as Sapta Sindhu.

FEATURES
• Society was primarily pastoral with cattle as the main measure of wealth
• Important term Gavishti refers to search for cows and also warfare
• Political organisation was tribal in nature based on Jana and Vish
• Raja was a tribal chief and not an absolute monarch
• Sabha and Samiti were important assemblies controlling the king
• Economy was based on cattle rearing with limited agriculture
• No clear evidence of private land ownership

RIVERS
• Early Vedic geography is associated with rivers like Indus, Saraswati and its tributaries
• Saraswati is frequently mentioned in Rigveda

RELIGION
• Nature worship dominated with gods like Indra, Agni and Varuna
• No temples or idol worship
• Simple rituals and offerings were performed

LATER VEDIC AGE
The Later Vedic period roughly spans from 1000 BCE to 600 BCE. Aryans moved eastwards towards the Ganga Yamuna plains.

FEATURES
• Shift from pastoral economy to agriculture based economy
• Use of iron tools helped in forest clearing and expansion
• Emergence of territorial kingdoms replacing tribal units
• King became more powerful and position became hereditary
• Decline of Sabha and Samiti influence

POLITY
• Larger political units called Janapadas developed
• Bali or tax collection became more regular
• Administrative machinery became more structured

SOCIETY
• Varna system became more rigid and hierarchical
• Four varnas Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra became clearly defined
• Position of women declined compared to Early Vedic period

ECONOMY
• Agriculture became dominant with crops like rice and barley
• Crafts and trade expanded
• Use of iron tools increased productivity

RELIGION
• Rituals became more complex and elaborate
• Dominance of Brahmanas increased
• Emergence of concepts like karma and rebirth
• Later texts such as Brahmanas and Upanishads reflect philosophical developments

SIGNIFICANCE
The Vedic Age laid the foundation of Indian society, religion and political institutions. The transition from tribal to territorial organisation and from pastoral to agricultural economy shaped later historical developments.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Early Vedic society was pastoral while Later Vedic was agricultural
• Sabha and Samiti were important in Early Vedic polity
• Varna system became rigid in Later Vedic period
• Iron technology played a key role in expansion into Ganga plains
• Saraswati river is central in Early Vedic geography

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often confuses Early and Later Vedic features. Sabha and Samiti are prominent in Early Vedic period, while strong monarchy, agriculture dominance and rigid varna system belong to Later Vedic period.
Ancient History.Buddhism:
INTRODUCTION
Buddhism was founded by Gautama Buddha in the 6th century BCE as a reform movement against ritualism and social inequalities of Later Vedic society. It emphasized ethical conduct, meditation and wisdom.

BUDDHA
• Born as Siddhartha in Lumbini
• Belonged to Shakya clan
• Attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya under the Bodhi tree
• Delivered first sermon at Sarnath known as Dharmachakra Pravartana
• Attained Mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar

CORE DOCTRINES
• Four Noble Truths
1. Life is full of suffering Dukkha
2. Cause of suffering is desire Trishna
3. Suffering can be ended
4. Path to end suffering is Eightfold Path

EIGHTFOLD PATH
• Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration

PHILOSOPHICAL IDEAS
• Anitya meaning impermanence
• Anatma meaning no permanent soul
• Nirvana meaning liberation from cycle of birth and death

FEATURES
• Rejected authority of Vedas and rituals
• Opposed caste system and social hierarchy
• Emphasized middle path avoiding extremes
• Promoted ethical living and compassion

BUDDHIST TEXTS
• Tripitaka consists of Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka and Abhidhamma Pitaka

BUDDHIST COUNCILS
• First Council at Rajagriha under Ajatashatru
• Second Council at Vaishali led to differences
• Third Council at Pataliputra under Ashoka
• Fourth Council at Kundalvana in Kashmir under Kanishka

SECTS
• Hinayana focuses on individual salvation and original teachings
• Mahayana emphasizes Bodhisattva ideal and worship of Buddha as divine

SPREAD OF BUDDHISM
• Ashoka played a major role in spreading Buddhism
• Spread to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and South East Asia
• Missionaries like Mahinda carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka

SIGNIFICANCE
Buddhism challenged social inequalities and promoted moral values. It contributed to art, architecture and spread of Indian culture beyond India.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Four Noble Truths form the foundation of Buddhism
• Eightfold Path provides practical approach to liberation
• Ashoka was key patron of Buddhism
• Tripitaka is the main source of teachings
• Mahayana introduced idol worship and Bodhisattva concept

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks differences between Hinayana and Mahayana. Idol worship and Bodhisattva concept belong to Mahayana, not original Buddhism.
Ancient History.Jainism:
INTRODUCTION
Jainism was founded as a reform movement against ritualism and social inequalities of Later Vedic period. It was systematized by Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, in the 6th century BCE.

MAHAVIRA
• Born at Kundagrama near Vaishali
• Belonged to Kshatriya clan
• Renounced worldly life at the age of 30
• Attained Kevala Jnana meaning supreme knowledge
• Attained Nirvana at Pavapuri

CORE DOCTRINES
• Triratna or Three Jewels
1. Right faith
2. Right knowledge
3. Right conduct

FIVE VOWS
• Ahimsa non violence
• Satya truth
• Asteya non stealing
• Aparigraha non possession
• Brahmacharya celibacy

PHILOSOPHICAL IDEAS
• Anekantavada meaning reality is multi sided
• Syadvada meaning conditional assertion
• Strong emphasis on non violence in thought, word and action

FEATURES
• Rejected authority of Vedas and rituals
• Opposed caste system
• Practiced extreme asceticism
• Stressed strict ethical discipline

SECTS
• Digambara meaning sky clad monks do not wear clothes and believe women cannot attain liberation
• Svetambara meaning white clad monks wear clothes and accept possibility of liberation for women

TEXTS
• Jain literature is called Agamas
• Composed mainly in Prakrit language

PRACTICES
• Sallekhana is ritual fasting unto death
• Emphasis on non violence led to vegetarianism

SPREAD
• Supported by rulers like Chandragupta Maurya in later life
• Spread mainly in western and southern India

SIGNIFICANCE
Jainism contributed to ethical values, non violence and simplicity. It influenced Indian philosophy, art and architecture.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara
• Triratna is central to Jain philosophy
• Anekantavada is a key philosophical concept
• Jainism emphasizes strict asceticism compared to Buddhism
• Digambara and Svetambara differ on clothing and role of women

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often confuses Jainism and Buddhism. Extreme asceticism and strict non violence are more associated with Jainism, while Buddhism follows the middle path.
Ancient History.Mahajanapadas:
INTRODUCTION
Around the 6th century BCE, several large states known as Mahajanapadas emerged in northern India. This period marks the transition from tribal polity to territorial states.

FEATURES
• Total 16 Mahajanapadas are mentioned in Buddhist texts like Anguttara Nikaya
• Located mainly in the Indo Gangetic plains
• Two types of political systems existed monarchy and republic
• Rise of cities and trade centres

IMPORTANT MAHAJANAPADAS
• Magadha with capital at Rajagriha and later Pataliputra
• Kosala with capital at Shravasti
• Vatsa with capital at Kaushambi
• Avanti with capital at Ujjain
• Anga with capital at Champa

REPUBLICAN STATES
• Vajji confederacy with capital at Vaishali
• Malla with centres at Kushinagar and Pava
• These were known as Gana Sanghas where power was shared among members

POLITY
• Monarchies had hereditary kings with administrative machinery
• Republics had assemblies and councils
• Decisions were taken collectively in republican states

ECONOMY
• Agriculture expanded due to iron tools
• Trade and commerce developed with emergence of towns
• Use of punch marked coins began

RISE OF MAGADHA
Magadha became the most powerful Mahajanapada due to several advantages

FACTORS
• Fertile alluvial soil of Ganga plains
• Availability of iron ore in nearby regions
• Strategic location with river transport
• Strong rulers like Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and later Mahapadma Nanda

SIGNIFICANCE
The Mahajanapada period laid the foundation for large empires in India. It also provided the background for the rise of Buddhism and Jainism.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• 16 Mahajanapadas existed in 6th century BCE
• Magadha emerged as the most powerful state
• Vajji and Malla were important republics
• Capitals and locations are important for exams
• Iron technology played a key role in expansion

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about republican states. Vajji and Malla were republics, while Magadha and Kosala were monarchies.
Ancient History.Mauryan Empire:
INTRODUCTION
The Mauryan Empire was the first large scale empire in Indian history founded by Chandragupta Maurya in the 4th century BCE. It established political unity and a highly centralized administrative system.

CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA
• Founded the empire with the guidance of Chanakya also known as Kautilya
• Defeated the Nanda dynasty and established capital at Pataliputra
• Defeated Seleucus Nicator and gained north western territories
• Greek ambassador Megasthenes visited his court and wrote Indica

ARTHASHASTRA
• Written by Kautilya, it deals with statecraft, administration and economy
• Mentions Saptanga theory of state king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army and allies
• Emphasizes strong central authority and efficient bureaucracy

BINDUSARA
• Son of Chandragupta Maurya
• Expanded empire towards Deccan region
• Maintained administrative structure

ASHOKA
• Greatest Mauryan ruler known for transformation after Kalinga War
• Kalinga War highlighted in Major Rock Edict 13
• Adopted policy of Dhamma and promoted moral governance

ASHOKA DHAMMA
• Focused on non violence, tolerance, respect for elders and compassion
• Not identical to Buddhism, it was a broader ethical policy
• Promoted welfare measures such as medical facilities and roads

INSCRIPTIONS
• Rock edicts and pillar edicts are primary sources
• Written mainly in Prakrit using Brahmi script
• In north western region inscriptions found in Greek and Aramaic
• Important sites include Girnar, Dhauli, Sarnath and Sanchi

ADMINISTRATION
• Highly centralized with king as supreme authority
• Council of ministers assisted governance
• Empire divided into provinces like Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri
• Governors were often royal princes

OFFICIALS
• Samaharta was chief revenue collector
• Sannidhata was treasurer
• Amatyas were high officials

ESPIONAGE SYSTEM
• Well developed spy system
• Spies included disguised agents such as ascetics, merchants and householders
• Used for internal security and surveillance

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation
• Land revenue was main source of income
• State controlled mining, forests and trade
• Use of punch marked coins for transactions

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
• Polished stone pillars known for Mauryan polish
• Sarnath Lion Capital is national emblem
• Stupas like Sanchi and Bharhut developed

SIGNIFICANCE
Mauryan Empire laid foundation of centralized governance, economic control and imperial administration. Ashoka's Dhamma spread ideas of ethical rule and peace.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• First political unification under Mauryas
• Arthashastra provides administrative details
• Ashoka inscriptions are key sources
• Provinces governed by princes
• Greek and Aramaic inscriptions found in north west

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often confuses Dhamma with Buddhism. Ashoka's Dhamma was an ethical policy and not strict propagation of Buddhism.
Ancient History.Indo Greeks:
INTRODUCTION
The Indo Greeks were among the earliest foreign rulers to establish their control in north western India after the decline of the Mauryan Empire. They were of Greek origin and are also known as Yavanas.

ORIGIN
• Indo Greeks were successors of Alexander's generals
• Established control in Bactria and later expanded into India
• Entered India around 2nd century BCE

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Demetrius was the first Indo Greek ruler to invade India
• Menander also known as Milinda was the most famous ruler
• Menander is associated with the Buddhist text Milinda Panha

MENANDER
• Ruled from capital at Sagala modern Sialkot
• Converted to Buddhism according to tradition
• Engaged in philosophical dialogue with Nagasena

ADMINISTRATION AND FEATURES
• Maintained Greek style administration along with Indian practices
• Promoted trade and urban centres in north western region

COINAGE
• Issued high quality coins
• Coins were bilingual with Greek and Kharosthi scripts
• First rulers to issue realistic portrait coins in India
• Helped in development of monetary economy

RELIGION
• Initially followed Greek deities
• Later rulers showed patronage to Buddhism
• Cultural interaction between Greek and Indian traditions

ART AND CULTURE
• Contributed to development of Gandhara art
• Blend of Greek and Indian artistic styles
• Realistic human figures and use of stone sculpture

SIGNIFICANCE
Indo Greeks contributed to cultural exchange, coinage development and spread of Buddhism. They played a role in connecting India with the Hellenistic world.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Known as Yavanas in Indian sources
• Menander is the most important Indo Greek ruler
• Bilingual coins are a key feature
• Associated with Gandhara art development
• Controlled north western India

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often links Indo Greeks with coinage. They introduced portrait coins and bilingual inscriptions in Greek and Kharosthi scripts.
Ancient History.Sakas:
INTRODUCTION
The Shakas were Central Asian tribes also known as Scythians who entered India after the Indo Greeks. They established their rule mainly in western India.

ORIGIN
• Originated from Central Asia
• Migrated into India due to pressure from other tribes
• Entered India around 1st century BCE

POLITICAL SYSTEM
• Adopted the title Kshatrapa meaning governor
• Higher title Mahakshatrapa was used for supreme rulers
• This system is known as Satrap system

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Rudradaman I was the most important Shaka ruler
• Issued Junagadh inscription in Sanskrit
• Known for repairing Sudarshana Lake

ADMINISTRATION
• Followed decentralized administration under satraps
• Regions governed by Kshatrapas under central authority

COINAGE
• Continued use of coins with Greek influence
• Coins carried ruler names and symbols

RELIGION AND CULTURE
• Patronized Hinduism and Buddhism
• Played role in spread of Indian culture
• Use of Sanskrit in inscriptions increased

SAKA ERA
• Saka Era began in 78 CE
• Later adopted as official calendar in India

GEOGRAPHICAL CONTROL
• Dominated regions like Gujarat, Malwa and western India
• Western Kshatrapas were prominent branch

SIGNIFICANCE
Shakas contributed to political developments, coinage and cultural integration. They played a key role in transition between Indo Greeks and Kushanas.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Known as Scythians of Central Asian origin
• Used titles Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa
• Rudradaman is most important ruler
• Junagadh inscription is first major Sanskrit inscription
• Saka Era begins in 78 CE

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Saka Era and titles. Kshatrapa system is associated with Shakas, not Mauryas or Guptas.
Ancient History.Kushanas:
INTRODUCTION
The Kushanas were one of the most important Central Asian tribes who established a powerful empire in north western India and Central Asia after the Shakas.

ORIGIN
• Originally part of Yuezhi tribes of Central Asia
• Migrated into India after displacing other tribes
• Established rule around 1st century CE

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Kujula Kadphises founded Kushana power in India
• Vima Kadphises expanded the empire and issued gold coins
• Kanishka was the greatest ruler of Kushana dynasty

KANISHKA
• Capital at Purushapura modern Peshawar
• Famous for patronage of Buddhism
• Convened Fourth Buddhist Council at Kundalvana in Kashmir
• Supported spread of Mahayana Buddhism

RELIGION
• Patronized multiple religions including Buddhism, Hinduism and Iranian deities
• Mahayana Buddhism flourished during this period

BUDDHISM
• Mahayana emphasized Bodhisattva ideal and idol worship
• Buddhism spread to Central Asia and China through Kushanas

ECONOMY AND TRADE
• Controlled important trade routes including Silk Route
• Trade linked India with Central Asia, Rome and China
• Issued large number of gold coins indicating prosperous economy

ART AND CULTURE
• Gandhara art shows Greek influence with realistic features
• Mathura art shows indigenous Indian style
• Development of Buddha images in human form

SIGNIFICANCE
Kushanas played a major role in spread of Buddhism and cultural exchange between India and Central Asia. They strengthened trade networks and artistic developments.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Originated from Yuezhi tribes
• Kanishka is the most important ruler
• Fourth Buddhist Council associated with Kanishka
• Silk Route trade flourished
• Gandhara and Mathura art developed

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often links Kanishka with Mahayana Buddhism and Fourth Buddhist Council. These are key identifiers of Kushana period.
Ancient History.Kalinga Kharavela:
INTRODUCTION
Kharavela was an important ruler of Kalinga belonging to the Mahameghavahana dynasty. He is known mainly from the Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri in Odisha.

SOURCE
• Hathigumpha inscription is the primary source of information
• Written in Prakrit language using Brahmi script
• Provides details of his achievements and administration

DYNASTY
• Belonged to Mahameghavahana dynasty
• Ruled in 1st century BCE

ACHIEVEMENTS
• Undertook military campaigns in different regions
• Defeated rulers of Magadha and other areas
• Restored Kalinga’s power after Mauryan decline

PUBLIC WORKS
• Promoted irrigation and repaired canals
• Encouraged urban development and infrastructure

RELIGION
• Patron of Jainism
• Supported Jain monks and religious activities
• Promoted religious tolerance

ADMINISTRATION
• Strong and efficient ruler with focus on welfare
• Balanced military expansion with public development

SIGNIFICANCE
Kharavela revived the political power of Kalinga and contributed to cultural and religious developments. His rule reflects regional assertion after Mauryan decline.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Known from Hathigumpha inscription
• Belonged to Mahameghavahana dynasty
• Patron of Jainism
• Promoted irrigation and public works
• Ruled in 1st century BCE

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Hathigumpha inscription. It is associated with Kharavela of Kalinga, not with Mauryas or Guptas.
Ancient History.Satavahanas:
INTRODUCTION
The Satavahanas were an important dynasty in the Deccan region after the Mauryan decline. They acted as a bridge between northern and southern India.

ORIGIN
• Known as Andhra dynasty in Puranas
• Established rule in Deccan around 1st century BCE
• Capital at Pratishthana modern Paithan

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Simuka was the founder of Satavahana dynasty
• Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest ruler
• Defeated Shakas and restored Satavahana power

GAUTAMIPUTRA SATAKARNI
• Known from Nasik inscription
• Assumed title of Eka Brahmana meaning sole Brahmana
• Upheld social order and varna system

ADMINISTRATION
• Decentralized administration with local governors
• Use of titles like Maharathi and Mahabhoja
• Land grants given to Brahmanas and religious institutions

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation
• Active inland and maritime trade
• Trade with Roman Empire flourished
• Ports like Kalyan and Sopara were important

COINAGE
• Issued coins mainly in lead and copper
• Coins often had Prakrit legends

RELIGION
• Patronized both Brahmanism and Buddhism
• Donated to Buddhist monasteries and stupas
• Religious tolerance was followed

SOCIETY
• Matrilineal naming system seen in rulers names like Gautamiputra
• Indicates importance of mother’s lineage

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
• Development of rock cut caves like Nasik and Karle
• Stupas at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda flourished

SIGNIFICANCE
Satavahanas played a key role in Deccan political history, trade expansion and cultural integration. They linked northern and southern India.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Known as Andhra dynasty
• Gautamiputra Satakarni is most important ruler
• Nasik inscription is key source
• Trade with Romans flourished
• Matrilineal naming pattern is unique feature

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Gautamiputra Satakarni and Nasik inscription. Matrilineal naming pattern is a key identifying feature of Satavahanas.
Ancient History.Sangam Age:
INTRODUCTION
The Sangam Age refers to the early historic period of South India mainly in Tamil region. It is known from Sangam literature composed by Tamil poets and provides valuable information about society, economy and polity.

SOURCES
• Sangam literature is main source
• Divided into Ettuthokai Eight Anthologies and Pattuppattu Ten Idylls
• Tolkappiyam is earliest Tamil grammar and gives social and political details
• Foreign accounts like Periplus of the Erythraean Sea provide trade information

POLITICAL ORGANIZATION
• Three major kingdoms Chera, Chola and Pandya
• Cheras controlled western Tamil region and Kerala
• Cholas ruled from Uraiyur and later Kaveripattinam
• Pandyas ruled from Madurai
• Kings were supported by chiefs called Velirs

ADMINISTRATION
• Monarchical system with king as supreme authority
• Local administration handled by assemblies and officials
• No elaborate bureaucracy like Mauryas

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation with rice as staple crop
• Extensive inland and overseas trade
• Trade with Roman Empire was significant
• Ports like Muziris, Arikamedu and Kaveripattinam were important
• Roman gold coins found in South India

SOCIETY
• Society was clan based with importance to kinship
• Divided into occupational groups
• Women had relatively better status compared to north India
• Practice of hero stones Nadukal for warriors

TINAI CONCEPT
• Land classified into five regions Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neital and Palai
• Each region associated with specific occupation and lifestyle

RELIGION
• Worship of nature and local deities
• Murugan and Korravai were important deities
• Later influence of Brahmanism and Jainism seen

ART AND CULTURE
• Rich tradition of poetry and literature
• Sangam poems reflect daily life, war and love themes
• Music and dance were popular

SIGNIFICANCE
Sangam Age provides earliest historical account of South India. It highlights trade, culture and political organization of Tamil region.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Sangam literature is primary source
• Three kingdoms Chera, Chola and Pandya
• Trade with Romans was extensive
• Tinai concept explains land classification
• Hero stones Nadukal represent warrior culture

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Sangam literature and trade. Roman trade and ports like Muziris are key features of Sangam Age.
Ancient History.Gupta Empire:
INTRODUCTION
The Gupta Empire established in the 4th century CE is considered the Golden Age of ancient India due to advancements in administration, economy, science and culture.

FOUNDATION
• Founded by Sri Gupta
• Chandragupta I laid foundation of Gupta power
• Adopted title Maharajadhiraja
• Established capital at Pataliputra

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Samudragupta known as Napoleon of India for his military conquests
• Prayag Prashasti inscription by Harisena describes his achievements
• Chandragupta II also known as Vikramaditya expanded empire and defeated Shakas

ADMINISTRATION
• Decentralized administration compared to Mauryas
• Empire divided into provinces called Bhuktis
• Provinces subdivided into Vishayas and villages
• Local administration gained importance

LAND GRANTS
• Practice of granting land to Brahmanas and officials increased
• Led to emergence of feudal tendencies
• Reduced direct control of central authority

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation
• Extensive use of gold coins known as Dinaras
• Trade and commerce flourished though later declined

SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
• Aryabhata contributed to mathematics and astronomy
• Proposed rotation of Earth and value of pi
• Varahamihira contributed to astronomy and astrology

LITERATURE
• Sanskrit literature flourished
• Kalidasa composed works like Abhijnanasakuntalam
• Puranas and Smritis were compiled

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
• Development of temple architecture in stone
• Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is example
• Ajanta caves paintings reached peak
• Sarnath school of sculpture developed

RELIGION
• Revival of Brahmanism
• Growth of Vaishnavism and Shaivism
• Religious tolerance continued

FOREIGN ACCOUNT
• Chinese traveler Fa Hien visited India during Gupta period
• Described prosperity and social conditions

SIGNIFICANCE
Gupta period is called Golden Age due to achievements in science, art, literature and stable administration. It marked high cultural development in India.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Samudragupta Prayag Prashasti is key source
• Gold coins Dinaras are important feature
• Aryabhata contributed to science
• Decentralized administration with land grants
• Fa Hien account describes Gupta society

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks difference between Mauryan and Gupta administration. Mauryas were highly centralized while Guptas followed decentralized system with land grants.
Ancient History.Harsha Era:
INTRODUCTION
The Harsha Era marks the rule of Harshavardhana in the 7th century CE after the decline of the Gupta Empire. It represents a period of political consolidation in north India.

DYNASTY
• Belonged to Pushyabhuti dynasty
• Capital initially at Thanesar and later shifted to Kannauj

HARSHAVARDHANA
• Ascended throne in 606 CE
• Unified large parts of north India
• Maintained diplomatic relations with foreign rulers

SOURCES
• Harshacharita written by Banabhatta provides details of his life
• Chinese traveler Xuanzang visited his court and described administration and society

ADMINISTRATION
• Monarchical system with king as supreme authority
• Decentralized administration similar to Guptas
• Officials managed provinces and local regions
• Army consisted of infantry, cavalry and elephants

RELIGION
• Initially follower of Shaivism later became patron of Buddhism
• Promoted religious tolerance
• Organized religious assemblies

ASSEMBLIES
• Kannauj assembly for religious discussions
• Prayag assembly held every five years for charity and distribution of wealth

ECONOMY
• Agriculture remained main occupation
• Trade and commerce continued but not as strong as Gupta period

CULTURE
• Patron of scholars like Banabhatta
• Nalanda University flourished during his time
• Encouraged art and learning

DECLINE
• Empire weakened after his death
• No strong successor led to fragmentation

SIGNIFICANCE
Harsha was the last great ruler of ancient north India before regional kingdoms emerged. His reign reflects continuity of classical traditions with emerging medieval trends.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Belonged to Pushyabhuti dynasty
• Harshacharita and Xuanzang are key sources
• Kannauj became political centre
• Organized religious assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag
• Nalanda University flourished

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often links Xuanzang with Harsha period. He visited during Harsha reign and described administration and society in detail.
Ancient History.Badami Chalukyas:
INTRODUCTION
The Badami Chalukyas were an important dynasty of early medieval India who ruled the Deccan region between the 6th and 8th centuries CE. Their capital was at Vatapi modern Badami.

FOUNDATION
• Founded by Pulakeshin I
• Established capital at Badami in Karnataka

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Pulakeshin II was the greatest ruler of the dynasty
• Defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of river Narmada
• Expanded empire over large parts of Deccan

SOURCES
• Aihole inscription written by Ravikirti describes achievements of Pulakeshin II
• Provides valuable historical information about the dynasty

ADMINISTRATION
• Monarchical system with king as supreme authority
• Empire divided into provinces and districts
• Local administration handled by officials and village assemblies
• Land grants were given to Brahmanas and temples

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation
• Trade and commerce developed in Deccan region

RELIGION
• Patronized Hinduism mainly Shaivism and Vaishnavism
• Also supported Jainism and Buddhism
• Religious tolerance was followed

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
• Known for development of Vesara style which is combination of Nagara and Dravida styles
• Rock cut temples at Badami
• Structural temples at Aihole and Pattadakal
• Pattadakal is UNESCO World Heritage site

SIGNIFICANCE
The Badami Chalukyas played a major role in political consolidation of Deccan and development of temple architecture. They contributed to cultural synthesis in India.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Capital at Badami
• Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha
• Aihole inscription is key source
• Vesara style of architecture developed
• Temples at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal are important

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Vesara style. It is associated with Chalukyas and is a mix of Nagara and Dravida styles.
Ancient History.Pallavas:
INTRODUCTION
The Pallavas were an important dynasty of South India who ruled parts of Tamil Nadu and Andhra region between the 6th and 9th centuries CE. Their capital was at Kanchipuram.

IMPORTANT RULERS
• Mahendravarman I initiated rock cut temple architecture
• Narasimhavarman I also known as Mamalla defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Vatapi
• Narasimhavarman II built Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram

ADMINISTRATION
• Monarchical system with king as supreme authority
• Provinces administered by officials
• Village assemblies played role in local governance
• Land grants given to Brahmanas and temples

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation
• Trade and commerce flourished especially coastal trade

RELIGION
• Patronized Hinduism mainly Shaivism and Vaishnavism
• Also supported Jainism and Buddhism
• Religious tolerance was practiced

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
• Known for development of Dravida style temple architecture
• Rock cut temples at Mahabalipuram
• Structural temples like Shore Temple
• Pancha Rathas are monolithic rock cut temples
• Transition from rock cut to structural temples seen clearly

CULTURE
• Kanchipuram became a major cultural and educational centre
• Sanskrit and Tamil literature flourished

SIGNIFICANCE
Pallavas played a key role in development of South Indian temple architecture and cultural growth. Their contribution influenced later Chola architecture.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Capital at Kanchipuram
• Narasimhavarman I defeated Chalukyas
• Mahabalipuram monuments are important
• Transition from rock cut to structural temples
• Dravida style developed

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Mahabalipuram monuments. Pancha Rathas and Shore Temple are associated with Pallavas, not Cholas.

Medieval History.Rajput Kingdoms:
INTRODUCTION
After the decline of Harsha Empire in the 7th century CE, north India witnessed the emergence of several regional kingdoms known as Rajput states. This period is marked by political fragmentation and rise of warrior clans.

ORIGIN OF RAJPUTS
• Various theories exist regarding origin
• Agnikula theory mentions origin from fire ritual at Mount Abu
• Some historians link them to foreign tribes like Hunas
• Others consider them as descendants of ancient Kshatriyas

MAJOR RAJPUT CLANS
• Chauhans ruled Ajmer and Delhi
• Solankis or Chalukyas ruled Gujarat
• Paramaras ruled Malwa
• Chandellas ruled Bundelkhand
• Gahadavalas ruled Kannauj

POLITICAL STRUCTURE
• Feudal system dominated polity
• King was supreme but depended on samantas feudatories
• Samantas provided military support and governed local regions
• Frequent conflicts among Rajput states weakened unity

ADMINISTRATION
• Decentralized administration with local autonomy
• Land grants to Brahmanas and officials were common
• Village administration played important role

ECONOMY
• Agriculture was main occupation
• Land revenue was main source of income
• Trade declined compared to ancient period but local trade continued

SOCIETY
• Society was hierarchical based on caste system
• Rajputs followed warrior code of honor
• Practices like Jauhar and Sati were prevalent
• Women had limited role in public life

MILITARY
• Strong emphasis on valor and personal bravery
• Lack of strategic unity among kingdoms
• Cavalry and infantry formed main army

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
• Development of temple architecture in Nagara style
• Famous temples include Khajuraho by Chandellas
• Forts and palaces were built for defense

SIGNIFICANCE
Rajput period represents transition to medieval polity with feudal structure. It also contributed to development of regional cultures and architecture.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Emerged after decline of Harsha
• Feudal polity with samanta system
• Major clans Chauhans, Solankis, Paramaras
• Known for valor but lacked unity
• Temple architecture flourished

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Rajput polity. It was feudal with strong role of samantas, not centralized like Mauryas.
Medieval History.Palas and Senas:
INTRODUCTION
The Pala and Sena dynasties were the two major ruling houses of eastern India especially Bengal and Bihar between the 8th and 13th centuries CE. The Palas are known for their patronage of Buddhism and major monastic universities, while the Senas are associated with the revival of Brahmanical traditions and a more rigid social order.

PALAS DYNASTY
The Pala dynasty was founded by Gopala in the middle of the 8th century CE. He is said to have been elected by regional chiefs in a situation of political disorder, which is an important feature of early medieval eastern Indian history.

IMPORTANT RULERS
Gopala founded the dynasty and consolidated control over Bengal
Dharmapala greatly expanded Pala power and intervened in the struggle for Kannauj
Devapala represented the high point of Pala imperial power and extended influence into Assam and parts of Odisha
Mahipala revived the dynasty after a phase of decline

POLITICAL IMPORTANCE
The Palas were one of the three major powers in the Tripartite Struggle for control over Kannauj. The other two were the Gurjara Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas.

ADMINISTRATION
The Pala polity had strong feudal features
Local administration depended heavily on subordinate chiefs and samantas
Land grants to officials, Brahmanas and religious institutions were common
The empire was extensive but control over distant areas depended on loyalty of feudatories

RELIGION
The Palas were important patrons of Buddhism
They supported late Mahayana Buddhism especially its Vajrayana form
They also showed tolerance towards Brahmanical traditions
Under the Palas, eastern India became a major centre of Buddhist learning and Tantric Buddhist practice

EDUCATION AND MONASTERIES
Nalanda received major patronage under the Palas
Vikramashila was founded by Dharmapala and became a famous centre of Buddhist learning
Odantapuri and Somapura were also important monastic institutions
Atisha Dipankara, associated with the Pala realm, later played a major role in the spread of Buddhism to Tibet

ART AND CULTURE
Pala art is known for refined bronze images and black stone sculptures
Sculptures often depict Buddhist deities and reflect influence of Vajrayana iconography
Pala artistic traditions influenced Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia
The Somapura Mahavihara in present day Bangladesh is one of the most important architectural remains of the period

ECONOMY
Agriculture formed the economic base of the kingdom
The fertile plains of Bengal and Bihar supported agrarian expansion
Riverine routes and access to maritime trade helped commercial activity
Trade contacts existed with Tibet and Southeast Asia

DECLINE OF PALAS
Pala power weakened due to succession struggles and the rise of regional powers
Repeated external pressure and weakening control over feudatories reduced imperial authority
Eventually the Senas replaced the Palas in Bengal

SENAS DYNASTY
The Sena dynasty succeeded the Palas in Bengal and represented a shift in religious and social orientation. The dynasty was founded by Hemanta Sena.

IMPORTANT RULERS
Vijayasena expanded Sena authority over large parts of Bengal
Ballala Sena is associated with Kulinism and strengthening of Brahmanical social hierarchy
Lakshmana Sena was the last important ruler and his reign ended with the Turkish conquest of Bengal under Bakhtiyar Khalji

ADMINISTRATION
The Senas followed a monarchical system with strong emphasis on Brahmanical legitimacy
Land grants continued and Brahmanas enjoyed increased influence
Regional administration continued to rely on local intermediaries

RELIGION AND SOCIETY
The Senas were orthodox Hindu rulers
They promoted Brahmanism and supported Smriti based social order
Buddhism declined significantly in Bengal under their rule
Caste distinctions became sharper and Kulinism is associated with this period

CULTURE
Sanskrit learning flourished under Sena patronage
Court scholarship and Brahmanical learning received encouragement
The Sena phase reflects a stronger integration of Bengal into mainstream Brahmanical political culture

DECLINE OF SENAS
The Sena kingdom weakened in the face of Turkish military expansion
Bakhtiyar Khalji defeated Lakshmana Sena and captured Nadia, leading to the decline of Sena rule in Bengal

SIGNIFICANCE
The Palas made eastern India a major centre of Buddhist scholarship and international cultural exchange. The Senas represent the consolidation of Brahmanical social order in Bengal. Together these dynasties are crucial for understanding the political, religious and cultural history of early medieval eastern India.

IMPORTANT POINTS
The Palas were patrons of Mahayana Buddhism especially Vajrayana
Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and strengthened imperial expansion
The Palas were involved in the Tripartite Struggle
 Pala art influenced Tibet and Nepal
Ballala Sena is associated with Kulinism
Bakhtiyar Khalji ended Sena dominance in Bengal

PYQ TRAP
Nalanda, Vikramashila and Vajrayana Buddhism are linked mainly with the Palas, not the Senas. Kulinism is associated with the Senas, especially Ballala Sena, not with the Pala rulers.
Medieval History.Rashtrakutas:
INTRODUCTION
The Rashtrakutas were one of the most powerful dynasties of early medieval India who ruled large parts of the Deccan between the 8th and 10th centuries CE. They played a crucial role in the Tripartite Struggle for control over Kannauj and maintained extensive political and commercial contacts with regions outside India.

ORIGIN
The origin of the Rashtrakutas is debated but they are generally associated with the Deccan region. They rose to prominence under Dantidurga who overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami.

IMPORTANT RULERS
Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta power by defeating the Chalukyas
Krishna I consolidated the empire and built the famous Kailasa temple at Ellora
Dhruva Dharavarsha expanded the empire northwards and participated in the Tripartite Struggle
Govinda III achieved extensive military success and established supremacy over northern and southern powers
Amoghavarsha I was known for his long reign, cultural patronage and relatively peaceful rule

POLITICAL IMPORTANCE
The Rashtrakutas were one of the three major powers in the Tripartite Struggle along with the Gurjara Pratiharas and the Palas
They successfully controlled large parts of central India and Deccan and influenced northern politics

ADMINISTRATION
The administration was monarchical with strong feudal features
The empire was divided into rashtras, vishayas and villages
Local administration involved feudatories and officials
Land grants were widely given which strengthened feudal tendencies

ECONOMY
Agriculture was the backbone of the economy
Land revenue was the main source of income
Trade and commerce flourished due to strategic location between north and south India
Ports on the western coast facilitated overseas trade especially with the Arab world

TRADE AND FOREIGN CONTACTS
The Rashtrakutas maintained active trade relations with Arab merchants
Arab travelers like Sulaiman described the Rashtrakuta king as one of the most powerful rulers of the world
Horse trade and luxury goods trade were important aspects of commerce

RELIGION
The Rashtrakutas were generally tolerant rulers
They patronized Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Jainism
Amoghavarsha I was a follower of Jainism and supported Jain scholars

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
The Rashtrakutas made significant contributions to rock cut architecture
The Kailasa temple at Ellora built by Krishna I is a remarkable monolithic structure and represents the peak of rock cut architecture in India
Temple architecture under Rashtrakutas shows a blend of northern and southern styles

LITERATURE
Amoghavarsha I authored Kavirajamarga in Kannada which is one of the earliest works of Kannada literature
Sanskrit and Kannada literature flourished under Rashtrakuta patronage
Jain scholars were actively supported

DECLINE
The Rashtrakuta empire declined due to internal weaknesses and the rise of the Later Chalukyas
Loss of control over feudatories weakened central authority

SIGNIFICANCE
The Rashtrakutas played a key role in linking northern and southern India politically and economically. Their contributions to art, architecture and literature are significant in early medieval Indian history.

IMPORTANT POINTS
Rashtrakutas were key participants in the Tripartite Struggle
Kailasa temple at Ellora was built by Krishna I
Amoghavarsha I promoted Jainism and Kannada literature
Arab sources describe Rashtrakutas as powerful rulers

PYQ TRAP
Kailasa temple at Ellora is associated with Rashtrakutas not Pallavas or Cholas. Rashtrakutas were Deccan rulers but actively intervened in northern politics. Kavirajamarga is linked with Amoghavarsha I of Rashtrakutas not with Chalukyas or Pallavas.
Medieval History.Kalyani Chalukyas:
INTRODUCTION
The Kalyani Chalukyas also known as Western Chalukyas ruled the Deccan region between the 10th and 12th centuries CE after the decline of the Rashtrakutas. Their capital was at Kalyani modern Basavakalyan.

ORIGIN
They emerged after overthrowing the Rashtrakutas
Tailapa II is regarded as the founder of the Kalyani Chalukya power

IMPORTANT RULERS
Tailapa II established the dynasty and revived Chalukya power
Someshvara I strengthened the kingdom and shifted capital to Kalyani
Vikramaditya VI was the greatest ruler and his reign is known as Chalukya Vikrama era

VIKRAMADITYA VI
He had a long and stable reign
Introduced Vikrama era in 1076 CE
Patronized literature and scholars
Maintained control over large parts of Deccan

ADMINISTRATION
Monarchical system with feudal elements
Empire divided into provinces and districts
Local governance handled by feudatories and officials
Land grants were common and led to feudal tendencies

ECONOMY
Agriculture was the main occupation
Irrigation and land grants supported agrarian expansion
Trade and commerce connected Deccan with other regions

RELIGION
Patronized Shaivism and Vaishnavism
Also supported Jainism
Religious tolerance was a feature of their rule

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
Known for development of Later Chalukya or transitional style
This style represents a transition between early Chalukya and Hoysala architecture
Important temples at Lakkundi, Itagi and Gadag
Use of soapstone and intricate carvings became prominent

LITERATURE
Kannada and Sanskrit literature flourished
Bilhana wrote Vikramankadeva Charita praising Vikramaditya VI

DECLINE
Declined due to rise of Hoysalas and Yadavas
Weak successors could not maintain control over feudatories

SIGNIFICANCE
Kalyani Chalukyas acted as a link between early Chalukya and later Hoysala architecture. They played a key role in shaping the political and cultural landscape of the Deccan.

IMPORTANT POINTS
Tailapa II founded the dynasty
Vikramaditya VI is the most important ruler
Vikrama era begins in 1076 CE
Transitional temple architecture developed

PYQ TRAP
Kalyani Chalukyas are associated with transitional architecture between Chalukya and Hoysala styles not with pure Dravida or Nagara forms. Vikrama era is linked with Vikramaditya VI not with Gupta rulers.
Medieval History.Cholas:
INTRODUCTION
The Cholas were one of the most powerful dynasties of South India who ruled between the 9th and 13th centuries CE. They are known for their strong administration, naval power, temple architecture and efficient local self government.

ORIGIN
The Cholas were an ancient Tamil dynasty mentioned in Sangam literature
They rose to prominence under Vijayalaya Chola who captured Thanjavur

IMPORTANT RULERS
Rajaraja I expanded the empire and built Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur
Rajendra I extended Chola power to Southeast Asia and conducted naval expeditions
Kulottunga I maintained a vast empire and improved administration

ADMINISTRATION
Highly organized administrative system
Empire divided into Mandalam, Nadu, Kurram and villages
Strong central authority with effective local governance
Land survey and revenue assessment were systematic

LOCAL SELF GOVERNMENT
Village administration was highly developed
Sabha was assembly of Brahmana villages
Ur was assembly of non Brahmana villages
Nagaram represented merchant communities
Uttaramerur inscription provides detailed procedure of election and functioning of village assemblies

ECONOMY
Agriculture was main occupation supported by irrigation tanks and canals
Land revenue was main source of income
Temples acted as economic centers controlling land and resources
Active inland and overseas trade

TRADE AND NAVY
Cholas had a powerful navy
Maintained trade relations with Southeast Asia and China
Naval expeditions to Sri Lanka and Srivijaya empire
Merchant guilds like Manigramam and Ayyavole were active

RELIGION
Patronized Shaivism mainly but also supported Vaishnavism
Temples played central role in social and economic life
Religious tolerance existed

ART AND ARCHITECTURE
Dravida style of temple architecture reached its peak
Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur is a masterpiece
Development of bronze sculptures especially Nataraja image

LITERATURE
Tamil literature flourished
Saiva and Vaishnava devotional works expanded

DECLINE
Decline due to internal conflicts and rise of Pandyas and Hoysalas
Gradual weakening of central authority

SIGNIFICANCE
The Cholas represent the height of administrative efficiency, temple economy and maritime power in medieval India. Their local self government system is one of the most advanced in Indian history.

IMPORTANT POINTS
Rajaraja I and Rajendra I are most important rulers
Uttaramerur inscription explains local self government
Cholas had strong navy and overseas expansion
Temple centered economy was key feature
Dravida architecture reached peak under Cholas

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about local self government. Sabha, Ur and Nagaram are associated with Cholas not with Delhi Sultanate or Mughals. Uttaramerur inscription is key evidence of Chola village administration.
Medieval History.Emergence of Islam:
INTRODUCTION
Islam emerged in the 7th century CE in the Arabian Peninsula under Prophet Muhammad. It brought religious, social and political transformation in Arabia and later spread rapidly across Asia, Africa and parts of Europe.

PRE ISLAMIC ARABIA
Arab society was tribal and divided
Mecca was an important trade and religious center
Polytheism was widely practiced with Kaaba as central shrine
Society had social inequalities including slavery and low status of women

PROPHET MUHAMMAD
Born in Mecca around 570 CE
Received first revelation at Mecca at the age of 40
Preached monotheism and social equality
Faced opposition from Meccan elites

HIJRA
Migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE
Marks beginning of Islamic calendar
Established first Islamic community or Ummah

TEACHINGS OF ISLAM
Belief in one God Allah
Prophethood of Muhammad
Equality and brotherhood
Importance of charity and social justice
Five Pillars of Islam include faith, prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage

EXPANSION OF ISLAM
After death of Muhammad in 632 CE
Led by Caliphs who were successors of Prophet
Rapid expansion into West Asia, North Africa and Central Asia
Spread through conquest as well as trade and missionary activity

CALIPHATE
Political and religious leadership of Islamic world
Early Caliphs known as Rashidun Caliphs
Later Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates expanded empire further

ISLAM AND INDIA
Early contact through Arab traders on western coast of India
Sindh conquest by Muhammad bin Qasim in 8th century CE
Cultural and commercial exchanges followed

SIGNIFICANCE
Islam introduced new religious ideas of monotheism and equality
Played major role in shaping medieval world history and Indian history

IMPORTANT POINTS
Hijra in 622 CE marks beginning of Islamic calendar
Kaaba was central shrine even before Islam
Caliph is successor of Prophet Muhammad
Islam spread through both conquest and trade

PYQ TRAP
UPSC may confuse Hijra with birth or death of Prophet. Hijra marks the beginning of Islamic calendar. Early spread of Islam in India was through trade as well as conquest not only through invasions.
Medieval History.Arab Invasion of Sindh:
INTRODUCTION
The Arab invasion of Sindh in the early 8th century CE was the first successful Islamic military entry into the Indian subcontinent. It was led by Muhammad bin Qasim during the Umayyad Caliphate.

BACKGROUND
Arab traders had long-standing commercial contacts with the western coast of India
Political fragmentation in Sindh under Dahir made invasion easier
Immediate cause was the attack on Arab ships near the coast of Sindh

MUHAMMAD BIN QASIM
Young general of the Umayyad Caliphate
Invaded Sindh around 712 CE
Defeated Raja Dahir and established Arab control over Sindh

COURSE OF INVASION
Captured important towns like Debal, Brahmanabad and Multan
Used military strategies along with diplomacy
Allowed local population to practice their religion on payment of taxes

ADMINISTRATION
Introduced Islamic administration in conquered areas
Non Muslims were given status of protected people on payment of jizya
Local officials were often retained for governance

REASONS FOR LIMITED SUCCESS
Strong resistance from Indian rulers beyond Sindh
Distance from Arab centers of power
Internal issues within Umayyad Caliphate
Geographical barriers restricted expansion

IMPACT
First establishment of Islamic rule in India
Facilitated cultural and commercial exchanges between India and Arab world
Did not lead to immediate large scale political expansion in India

SIGNIFICANCE
Marked the beginning of long term interaction between Indian and Islamic civilizations
Sindh became a center for cultural exchange and transmission of knowledge

IMPORTANT POINTS
Muhammad bin Qasim invaded in 712 CE
Raja Dahir was ruler of Sindh defeated by Arabs
Arab rule remained limited mainly to Sindh and Multan

PYQ TRAP
UPSC may ask about extent of Arab success. Arabs were able to conquer only Sindh and parts of Multan and could not penetrate deep into India due to strong resistance and geographical factors.
Medieval History.Turkish Invasions:
INTRODUCTION
The Turkish invasions of India during the 11th and 12th centuries CE marked a major turning point in Indian history. Unlike the earlier Arab invasion which remained limited, the Turkish invasions led to the establishment of long lasting Islamic rule in North India.

BACKGROUND
Political fragmentation in North India after decline of Pratiharas
Presence of wealthy temples and cities attracted invaders
Weak military organization compared to Central Asian cavalry

MAHMUD OF GHAZNI
Conducted repeated raids between 1000 and 1027 CE
Attacked rich temples including Somnath
Objective was plunder and wealth not territorial expansion
Did not establish permanent rule in India

MUHAMMAD GHORI
Invaded India in late 12th century CE
Defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 CE
Laid foundation for permanent Turkish rule in India
Appointed Qutb ud din Aibak as his representative

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN MAHMUD AND GHORI
Mahmud aimed at plunder while Ghori aimed at conquest
Mahmud did not establish empire but Ghori laid foundation of Delhi Sultanate
Ghori's invasions had lasting political impact

CAUSES OF SUCCESS
Superior cavalry and use of mounted archers
Better military organization and mobility
Political disunity among Indian rulers
Lack of coordinated resistance

IMPACT
End of Rajput dominance in North India
Beginning of Turkish rule leading to Delhi Sultanate
Introduction of new military and administrative systems

SIGNIFICANCE
Turkish invasions resulted in establishment of centralized Islamic rule in India which continued for several centuries
Marked beginning of medieval phase of Indian history in political terms

IMPORTANT POINTS
Mahmud of Ghazni conducted raids not empire building
Muhammad Ghori laid foundation of Delhi Sultanate
Second Battle of Tarain 1192 CE is crucial event

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often confuses Mahmud and Ghori. Mahmud was mainly a raider while Ghori was a conqueror who established political control leading to Delhi Sultanate.
Medieval History.Slave Dynasty:
INTRODUCTION
The Slave Dynasty also known as Mamluk Dynasty was the first ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate from 1206 to 1290 CE. It was founded by Qutb ud din Aibak who was a former slave of Muhammad Ghori.

QUTB UD DIN AIBAK
Founder of the dynasty
Known as Lakh Baksh for his generosity
Started construction of Qutub Minar and Quwwat ul Islam mosque
His rule was short and consolidation was limited

ILTUTMISH
Real consolidator of Delhi Sultanate
Defeated rivals and secured Delhi throne
Introduced Iqta system for administration and revenue
Organized Chahalgani group of forty nobles
Received recognition from Abbasid Caliph
Completed Qutub Minar

RAZIA SULTAN
First and only woman ruler of Delhi Sultanate
Attempted to break power of Turkish nobles
Faced opposition from nobles and was overthrown

BALBAN
Strengthened monarchy and centralized power
Introduced theory of kingship based on divine right
Followed policy of blood and iron to suppress revolts
Crushed power of nobles and abolished Chahalgani
Strengthened army and administration

ADMINISTRATION
Iqta system formed backbone of administration
Iqta holders collected revenue and maintained troops
Strong centralized monarchy developed especially under Balban

CAUSES OF DECLINE
Weak successors after Balban
Internal conflicts among nobles
Rise of Khalji dynasty

SIGNIFICANCE
Laid foundation of Delhi Sultanate administration
Established centralized rule in North India
Developed administrative systems continued by later dynasties

IMPORTANT POINTS
Qutb ud din Aibak was founder
Iltutmish was real consolidator
Balban strengthened monarchy and crushed nobles
Iqta system was key administrative feature

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about Iqta system and Chahalgani. Iqta system was introduced by Iltutmish not by Balban. Balban actually reduced the power of nobles and abolished Chahalgani.
Medieval History.Khalji Dynasty:
INTRODUCTION
The Khalji Dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1290 to 1320 CE. It marked the end of Turkish monopoly and rise of a more inclusive ruling class. The dynasty is known for military expansion and strong economic reforms.

JALALUDDIN KHALJI
Founder of the dynasty
Adopted a mild and lenient policy
Faced internal conspiracies and was killed by Alauddin Khalji

ALAUDDIN KHALJI
Most powerful ruler of the dynasty
Expanded empire into Gujarat, Rajasthan and Deccan
Deccan campaigns led by Malik Kafur
Maintained a large standing army

MILITARY REFORMS
Introduced branding of horses and descriptive rolls of soldiers
Paid soldiers in cash salaries
Maintained strict discipline in army

MARKET CONTROL POLICY
Controlled prices of essential commodities
Established separate markets for grain, cloth and horses
Appointed officials to regulate markets
Fixed prices to ensure low cost of maintaining large army
Strict punishments for violations

REVENUE REFORMS
Land revenue increased especially in Doab region
Measurement of land for proper assessment
Reduced power of intermediaries
State collected revenue directly from peasants

ANTI NOBILITY MEASURES
Confiscated wealth of nobles
Banned social gatherings and marriages among nobles without permission
Strengthened central authority

ADMINISTRATION
Centralized administration with strong control of Sultan
Efficient spy system to monitor officials and nobles

ECONOMY
Agriculture was main source of income
State control ensured stability of prices
Trade continued but under strict supervision

DECLINE
Weak successors after Alauddin Khalji
Internal conflicts and conspiracies
End of dynasty with rise of Tughlaqs

SIGNIFICANCE
Khalji period is known for strong centralization, military expansion and innovative economic reforms especially market control system

IMPORTANT POINTS
Alauddin Khalji is most important ruler
Market control policy is unique feature
Malik Kafur led Deccan campaigns
Revenue reforms strengthened state control

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about market reforms. Price control and market regulation were introduced by Alauddin Khalji not by Tughlaqs or Mughals. Branding of horses and cash salary system were part of his military reforms.
Medieval History.Tughlaq Dynasty:
INTRODUCTION
The Tughlaq Dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1320 to 1414 CE. It is known for ambitious experiments, administrative innovations and later decline of central authority.

GHYASUDDIN TUGHLAQ
Founder of the dynasty
Focused on consolidation and administrative order
Built Tughlaqabad fort

MUHAMMAD BIN TUGHLAQ
Most controversial ruler of Delhi Sultanate
Highly intelligent but policies failed due to poor execution

IMPORTANT POLICIES
Transfer of capital from Delhi to Daulatabad to control Deccan but failed due to hardship
Introduction of token currency to overcome shortage of silver but failed due to counterfeiting
Increase of taxation in Doab region which led to peasant revolts
Planned expeditions to Central Asia and Khurasan but not successful

CHARACTER OF RULE
Visionary but impractical implementation
Policies ahead of time but lacked administrative support

FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ
Adopted welfare oriented policies
Reduced taxes and provided relief to peasants
Constructed canals, gardens and public works
Promoted irrigation and agriculture

ADMINISTRATION UNDER FIROZ
Made offices hereditary which weakened central authority
Relied heavily on nobles and ulema
Promoted Islamic orthodoxy

DECLINE
Weak successors after Firoz Shah
Frequent revolts and loss of control over provinces
Invasion of Timur in 1398 weakened Delhi Sultanate severely

SIGNIFICANCE
Tughlaq period shows contrast between ambitious experimentation and administrative decline. It marks beginning of decentralization of Delhi Sultanate.

IMPORTANT POINTS
Muhammad bin Tughlaq known for failed experiments
Token currency and capital shift are key policies
Firoz Shah known for welfare measures but weakened central power
Timur invasion was major blow

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often confuses policies. Token currency and capital transfer were introduced by Muhammad bin Tughlaq not by Firoz Shah. Firoz Shah focused on welfare and irrigation not on radical experiments.
Medieval History.Sayyid Dynasty:
INTRODUCTION
The Sayyid Dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1414 to 1451 CE. It was a weak and short lived dynasty that emerged after the invasion of Timur which had severely weakened Delhi.

ORIGIN
Founded by Khizr Khan in 1414 CE
He was appointed as governor of Multan by Timur
Did not assume the title of Sultan and ruled as a subordinate of Timur

IMPORTANT RULERS
Khizr Khan established the dynasty but had limited authority
Mubarak Shah tried to strengthen control but faced revolts
Muhammad Shah and Alam Shah were weak rulers

ADMINISTRATION
Weak central authority
Relied on local chiefs and nobles
Could not effectively control provinces

POLITICAL CONDITION
Delhi Sultanate was highly fragmented
Many regions became independent
Continuous rebellions weakened the dynasty

DECLINE
Alam Shah voluntarily abdicated the throne
Power transferred to Bahlul Lodi in 1451 CE
Marked end of Sayyid rule

SIGNIFICANCE
Represents the weakest phase of Delhi Sultanate
Shows decline of centralized authority after Tughlaqs
Acts as transition between Tughlaq and Lodi dynasties

IMPORTANT POINTS
Khizr Khan was founder
Did not take title of Sultan initially
Timur invasion led to its emergence
Ended with rise of Lodi dynasty

PYQ TRAP
UPSC may confuse founders. Sayyid dynasty was founded by Khizr Khan after Timur invasion not by Lodi rulers. It represents decline phase not expansion phase of Delhi Sultanate.
Medieval History.Lodi Dynasty:
INTRODUCTION
The Lodi Dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1451 to 1526 CE. It was the last ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate and was of Afghan origin. It marked the transition from Sultanate to Mughal rule.

BAHLUL LODI
Founder of the dynasty
Established control over Delhi after Sayyid dynasty
Followed a policy of sharing power with Afghan nobles

SIKANDAR LODI
Strengthened the administration and expanded the empire
Founded the city of Agra
Improved revenue system and promoted agriculture
Maintained strong control over nobles

IBRAHIM LODI
Last ruler of the dynasty
Tried to centralize power and reduce influence of Afghan nobles
Faced revolts from nobles due to his autocratic policies

AFGHAN NATURE OF RULE
Afghan polity was based on tribal equality
Nobles expected to share power rather than absolute monarchy
Centralization attempts led to conflicts

ADMINISTRATION
Moderate centralization compared to earlier dynasties
Local chiefs and nobles played important role
Revenue system continued from earlier Sultanate practices

DECLINE
Conflict between Ibrahim Lodi and Afghan nobles
Daulat Khan Lodi invited Babur to invade India
Ibrahim Lodi was defeated in First Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE

SIGNIFICANCE
End of Delhi Sultanate and beginning of Mughal Empire
Introduced Afghan element in Indian polity
Battle of Panipat marked major political shift in Indian history

IMPORTANT POINTS
Bahlul Lodi founded the dynasty
Sikandar Lodi founded Agra
Ibrahim Lodi defeated by Babur in 1526 CE
Afghan system based on tribal equality

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often asks about transition to Mughal rule. Ibrahim Lodi was defeated by Babur in First Battle of Panipat 1526 CE not by any internal rebellion. Afghan polity differed from Turkish system as it emphasized sharing of power among nobles.
Medieval History.Vijayanagara Empire:
INTRODUCTION

The Vijayanagara Empire was one of the most powerful and culturally vibrant empires of medieval South India. Founded in 1336 CE, it acted as a strong bulwark against northern invasions and preserved indigenous political and cultural traditions. It played a key role in the revival of Hindu polity, temple architecture and regional economy.

FOUNDATION

• Founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I
• They were originally feudatories of the Kakatiyas and later served under the Delhi Sultanate
• Guided by the sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri
• Capital city was Vijayanagara also known as Hampi located on the banks of Tungabhadra river

DYNASTIES

• Sangama Dynasty was the founding dynasty
• Saluva Dynasty came to power after weakening of Sangamas
• Tuluva Dynasty was the most powerful phase especially under Krishnadevaraya
• Aravidu Dynasty was the last ruling dynasty after the decline of central authority

KRISHNADEVARAYA

• Krishnadevaraya was the greatest ruler of Vijayanagara Empire
• Belonged to Tuluva dynasty
• His reign is considered the golden age of the empire
• He defeated Bahmani successor states and expanded territory in Deccan and South India
• He wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu
• His court included Ashtadiggajas or eight eminent Telugu scholars

ADMINISTRATION

• Highly centralized monarchy with king as supreme authority
• Empire divided into provinces called Rajya or Mandala
• Provinces were governed by Nayakas who were military chiefs
• Nayankara system involved granting land in return for military service
• Local administration involved village assemblies and traditional institutions

MILITARY

• Strong infantry, cavalry and war elephants
• Fortifications and strategic defense played major role
• Use of artillery increased over time especially in later phase
• Constant conflicts with Bahmani kingdom and its successor states

ECONOMY

• Agriculture was the backbone supported by irrigation tanks and canals
• Major crops included rice, sugarcane, cotton and spices
• Trade flourished with Arabs, Portuguese and Southeast Asia
• Important ports included Goa, Calicut and Pulicat
• Gold coins called Varaha were issued

SOCIETY

• Society was stratified but relatively stable
• Women had relatively better status in royal and elite circles
• Devadasi system was prevalent in temples
• Education and learning were encouraged especially in temples and mathas

RELIGION

• Strong patronage to Hinduism especially Vaishnavism and Shaivism
• Religious tolerance was practiced, Jainism and Islam also existed
• Temples were major socio economic centers

ART AND ARCHITECTURE

• Vijayanagara architecture is known for massive structures and ornate carvings
• Notable features include gopurams, mandapas and pillared halls
• Hampi complex includes Virupaksha Temple and Vittala Temple
• Musical pillars of Vittala temple are unique architectural feature
• Combination of Dravidian and local styles

FOREIGN ACCOUNTS

• Accounts of travelers like Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz provide valuable information
• They described Vijayanagara as one of the richest cities in the world
• Detailed descriptions of markets, festivals and administration are available

DECLINE

• Decline began after the Battle of Talikota in 1565 CE
• Combined forces of Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara army
• Capital Hampi was destroyed and looted
• Aravidu dynasty continued but empire weakened significantly

SIGNIFICANCE

• Preserved South Indian culture and traditions during medieval period
• Acted as a buffer against northern invasions
• Promoted temple architecture, literature and regional languages
• Strengthened trade and economy in South India

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Founded in 1336 CE by Harihara and Bukka
• Capital was Hampi on Tungabhadra river
• Krishnadevaraya was the greatest ruler
• Nayankara system was key administrative feature
• Battle of Talikota in 1565 CE led to decline

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Nayankara system with Zamindari system. Nayakas were military chiefs granted land for service, not hereditary landlords like later Zamindars. Krishnadevaraya belongs to Tuluva dynasty, not Sangama dynasty.
Medieval History.Bahmani Kingdom:
INTRODUCTION

The Bahmani Kingdom was the first independent Islamic kingdom in the Deccan, founded in 1347 CE. It played a crucial role in shaping Deccan politics and was a constant rival of the Vijayanagara Empire. It laid the foundation for later Deccan Sultanates.

FOUNDATION

• Founded in 1347 CE by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah
• He was also known as Hasan Gangu
• Declared independence from Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
• Capital was initially Gulbarga later shifted to Bidar

ADMINISTRATION

• Sultan was the supreme authority
• Kingdom divided into provinces called Tarafs
• Each Taraf was governed by a Tarafdar
• Central administration included Wazir, Amir and other officials
• Strong military organization with cavalry and artillery

NOBILITY FACTIONS

• Two major groups: Deccanis and Afaqis
• Deccanis were local converts and old settlers
• Afaqis were foreign nobles from Persia, Central Asia and Arabia
• Continuous conflict between these groups weakened the state

MAHMUD GAWAN

• Mahmud Gawan was the most important minister of Bahmani Kingdom
• Served under Muhammad Shah III
• Introduced administrative reforms to strengthen the kingdom
• Divided the empire into smaller Tarafs for better control
• Introduced land measurement and revenue reforms
• Established a famous madrasa at Bidar
• Executed due to court conspiracies, which weakened the kingdom

MILITARY AND CONFLICTS

• Constant conflicts with Vijayanagara Empire over Raichur Doab
• Raichur Doab was a fertile and strategically important region between Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers
• Frequent wars drained resources of both kingdoms

ECONOMY

• Agriculture was the main occupation
• Trade flourished with Persian Gulf and Arabian regions
• Urban centers like Gulbarga and Bidar developed
• Use of irrigation and land revenue systems strengthened economy

CULTURE

• Persian culture had strong influence
• Development of Deccani language and literature
• Patronage to art, architecture and education
• Bidar became an important cultural center

ARCHITECTURE

• Bahmani architecture shows Persian influence
• Notable structures include Gulbarga Fort, Jama Masjid of Gulbarga and Bidar Fort
• Use of arches, domes and decorative styles

DECLINE

• Internal conflicts between Deccanis and Afaqis weakened the kingdom
• Weak successors after Mahmud Gawan
• By early 16th century, Bahmani Kingdom disintegrated
• It split into five Deccan Sultanates: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Berar

SIGNIFICANCE

• First major Islamic kingdom in Deccan
• Played key role in Deccan politics and culture
• Laid foundation for Deccan Sultanates
• Continuous rivalry with Vijayanagara shaped medieval South Indian history

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Founded in 1347 CE by Hasan Gangu Bahman Shah
• Capital shifted from Gulbarga to Bidar
• Mahmud Gawan was the greatest minister
• Conflict with Vijayanagara over Raichur Doab
• Declined into five Deccan Sultanates

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Deccanis and Afaqis. Deccanis were local Muslims while Afaqis were foreign nobles. Mahmud Gawan was a minister, not a ruler. Raichur Doab conflict was between Bahmani and Vijayanagara, not Delhi Sultanate.
Medieval History.Bhakti Movement:
INTRODUCTION
