The Bhakti Movement was a major socio religious reform movement in medieval India that emphasized personal devotion to God over ritualism. It emerged in different parts of India between the 7th and 17th centuries and played a crucial role in shaping Indian religious and cultural life.

ORIGIN AND EVOLUTION

• Originated in South India with Alvars and Nayanars between 7th and 9th centuries
• Later spread to North India from 13th century onwards
• Influenced by socio religious conditions including rigid caste system and ritualism
• Encouraged direct devotion without priestly mediation

SOUTH INDIAN TRADITION

• Alvars were Vaishnavite saints devoted to Vishnu
• Nayanars were Shaivite saints devoted to Shiva
• They composed devotional hymns in Tamil
• Strong opposition to caste discrimination and ritualism
• Important in spreading temple based devotional culture

NORTH INDIAN TRADITION

• Emerged from 13th century onwards
• Saints used vernacular languages to reach common people
• Two major streams: Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti

NIRGUNA BHAKTI

• Belief in formless God without attributes
• Rejected idol worship and rituals
• Emphasized inner devotion and equality
• Major saints included Kabir and Guru Nanak

SAGUNA BHAKTI

• Belief in God with form and attributes
• Devotion towards Rama or Krishna
• Emphasized love, surrender and devotion
• Major saints included Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

IMPORTANT SAINTS

• Kabir emphasized unity of God and criticized both Hindu and Muslim orthodoxy
• Guru Nanak founded Sikhism and emphasized equality and devotion
• Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi
• Surdas composed devotional songs on Krishna
• Mirabai was devoted to Krishna and rejected royal life
• Chaitanya promoted ecstatic devotion to Krishna in Bengal

PHILOSOPHICAL BASE

• Emphasis on Bhakti as the path to salvation
• Rejection of caste hierarchy in spiritual matters
• Focus on personal relationship between devotee and God
• Use of simple language and songs for communication

SOCIAL IMPACT

• Challenged caste discrimination and social inequalities
• Promoted equality and social harmony
• Encouraged use of regional languages leading to growth of literature
• Brought religion closer to common people

RELATION WITH SUFI MOVEMENT

• Bhakti and Sufi movements had similarities in emphasis on love and devotion
• Both opposed rigid orthodoxy and rituals
• Encouraged spiritual unity and tolerance

LIMITATIONS

• Did not completely eliminate caste system
• Influence remained limited in some regions
• Social change was gradual rather than revolutionary

SIGNIFICANCE

• Democratized religion by making it accessible to masses
• Strengthened regional languages and literature
• Promoted social reform and religious tolerance
• Left lasting cultural and spiritual legacy in India

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Origin in South India with Alvars and Nayanars
• Two streams: Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti
• Kabir and Nanak associated with Nirguna tradition
• Tulsidas, Surdas and Mirabai associated with Saguna tradition
• Emphasis on devotion over ritualism

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti. Nirguna means formless God and rejects idol worship, while Saguna accepts God with form like Rama or Krishna. Alvars were Vaishnavites and Nayanars were Shaivites.
Medieval History.Sufi Movement:
INTRODUCTION

The Sufi Movement was a mystical dimension of Islam that emphasized love, devotion and direct connection with God. It spread in India from the 12th century onwards and played a significant role in promoting spiritual harmony and cultural synthesis.

ORIGIN AND NATURE

• Originated in West Asia as a mystical tradition within Islam
• Emphasized inner spirituality over formal rituals and orthodoxy
• Focused on love, devotion and unity with God
• Sufis were organized into orders called Silsilah

KEY CONCEPTS

• Tauhid means unity of God
• Zikr refers to remembrance of God through repetition of divine names
• Sama refers to devotional music and singing
• Fana means annihilation of self in God
• Baqa means eternal existence with God

SILSILAHS OR ORDERS

• Chishti order was the most influential in India
• Suhrawardi order had closer relations with the state
• Qadiri and Naqshbandi orders emerged later
• Each Silsilah had its own spiritual practices and lineage

CHISHTI ORDER

• Founded in India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer
• Emphasized simplicity, poverty and service to humanity
• Maintained distance from political power
• Important saints include Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Nizamuddin Auliya and Baba Farid
• Use of music and devotional gatherings was common

SUHRAWARDI ORDER

• Founded by Shihabuddin Suhrawardi
• Maintained closer relations with rulers
• Accepted state patronage and official positions
• Important saint in India was Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan

NAQSHBANDI ORDER

• More orthodox and conservative
• Opposed practices like music and sama
• Supported strict adherence to Islamic law
• Associated with Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi

QADIRI ORDER

• Popular in later medieval period
• Less rigid compared to Naqshbandi
• Spread widely in different parts of India

IMPORTANT SAINTS

• Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti established Chishti order in India
• Nizamuddin Auliya was the most famous Chishti saint in Delhi
• Baba Farid contributed to Punjabi literature and Sikh scriptures
• Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi was associated with Naqshbandi order

PRACTICES

• Khanqahs were centers of Sufi activity
• Dargahs were tombs of Sufi saints and became pilgrimage centers
• Langar system provided food to followers and poor
• Emphasis on service, charity and equality

SOCIAL IMPACT

• Promoted communal harmony and tolerance
• Attracted followers from different religious backgrounds
• Reduced social divisions and caste barriers
• Encouraged use of local languages and cultural exchange

RELATION WITH STATE

• Chishti saints generally avoided political power
• Suhrawardi saints maintained relations with rulers
• Naqshbandi order supported orthodox policies of rulers like Aurangzeb

SIGNIFICANCE

• Strengthened cultural interaction between Hindu and Muslim communities
• Spread message of love, tolerance and unity
• Influenced Bhakti Movement and vice versa
• Played important role in Indian spiritual traditions

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sufism emphasizes love and devotion to God
• Organized into Silsilah or orders
• Chishti order most influential in India
• Khanqah is a Sufi center and Dargah is tomb of saint
• Zikr and Sama are important practices

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Chishti and Suhrawardi orders. Chishtis avoided political power and emphasized simplicity, while Suhrawardis accepted state patronage. Naqshbandi order opposed music and emphasized orthodoxy.
Medieval History.Early Mughals:
INTRODUCTION

The Mughal Empire was one of the most powerful and centralized empires in Indian history. It was founded in 1526 CE and shaped medieval Indian polity, economy, culture, architecture and administration. The Mughal phase is important not only for territorial expansion but also for imperial institutions such as Mansabdari, Jagirdari and revenue administration.

BABUR

• Babur founded the Mughal Empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE
• He defeated Rana Sanga in the Battle of Khanwa in 1527 CE and Medini Rai in the Battle of Chanderi in 1528 CE
• He used gunpowder, matchlocks and field artillery effectively in Indian warfare
• His memoir Tuzuk i Baburi or Baburnama is an important source
• His rule was short but he laid the military foundation of the empire

HUMAYUN

• Humayun faced constant resistance from Afghan chiefs and internal family rivalries
• He lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri after defeats at Chausa in 1539 CE and Kannauj in 1540 CE
• He spent years in exile and later regained the throne with Persian support in 1555 CE
• His reign is important because it shows the fragility of the early Mughal state

AKBAR

• Akbar was the real consolidator of the Mughal Empire
• He defeated Hemu in the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 CE
• He expanded Mughal authority over North India, Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir and parts of Deccan
• He abolished jizya for a period and followed Sulh i kul or universal peace
• He developed a strong centralized administration and brought Rajputs into imperial service
• His court historian Abul Fazl wrote Akbarnama and Ain i Akbari

ADMINISTRATION UNDER AKBAR

• The empire was divided into Suba, Sarkar, Pargana and village
• The emperor was supreme authority at the center
• Major central officers included Wazir, Mir Bakshi, Sadr us Sudur and Qazi
• Provincial administration was headed by Subahdar with separate financial and military officers
• This separation reduced concentration of power in one office

MANSABDARI SYSTEM

• Mansabdari system was introduced by Akbar
• Mansab meant rank and position in the imperial hierarchy
• Zat indicated personal status and salary
• Sawar indicated the number of cavalry to be maintained
• Mansabdars were appointed, promoted and transferred by the emperor
• This system combined civil and military service in one imperial framework

JAGIRDARI SYSTEM

• Jagir was a revenue assignment given to Mansabdars in place of cash salary
• Jagirdars did not own land permanently
• They were entitled to collect revenue from assigned areas on behalf of the state
• Frequent transfer of Jagirs was intended to prevent local power buildup
• In the later Mughal phase, Jagirdari crisis became an important factor in imperial decline

REVENUE SYSTEM

• Akbar's revenue administration was systematized under Raja Todar Mal
• Zabti system was based on measurement of land and assessment of average produce and prices
• Land was classified according to cultivation and productivity
• Dahsala system used ten year average for revenue assessment
• Revenue administration strengthened imperial finances and agrarian control

JAHANGIR

• Jahangir maintained the imperial structure built by Akbar
• He is associated with the chain of justice as a symbol of royal accessibility
• His reign saw the growing political influence of Nur Jahan
• Mughal painting reached refinement during his time, especially naturalistic studies of birds, animals and flowers
• English East India Company received permission to trade during this period

SHAH JAHAN

• Shah Jahan's reign is regarded as the period of Mughal architectural zenith
• He built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort of Delhi and Jama Masjid
• Imperial grandeur and court ceremonial reached high refinement
• Military campaigns continued in the Deccan and Central Asia frontier zones
• Heavy expenditure on architecture and warfare increased fiscal pressure

AURANGZEB

• Aurangzeb expanded the Mughal Empire to its maximum territorial extent
• He annexed Bijapur and Golconda and pursued long Deccan campaigns
• He reimposed jizya and followed a more orthodox religious policy than Akbar
• His reign faced revolts from Marathas, Jats, Sikhs and Satnamis
• Continuous warfare overextended the empire and weakened central control
• His period marks both territorial expansion and the beginning of serious imperial strain

ECONOMY

• Agriculture was the backbone of Mughal economy
• India produced wheat, rice, sugarcane, cotton and indigo on a large scale
• Textile production was highly developed and Indian textiles were in demand in world markets
• Urban centers such as Agra, Lahore, Delhi and Ahmedabad flourished
• Inland and overseas trade expanded under imperial stability

RELIGION AND IDEAS

• Akbar followed Sulh i kul based on tolerance and peace among all communities
• He discontinued pilgrimage tax and attempted to reduce religious discrimination
• Din i Ilahi was a small ethical order associated with Akbar and not a mass religion
• Aurangzeb's reign reflected greater orthodoxy and closer association with Islamic law

ART AND ARCHITECTURE

• Mughal architecture combined Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements
• Humayun's Tomb represents an early major example of Mughal architecture in India
• Fatehpur Sikri reflects Akbar's architectural vision
• Taj Mahal represents the peak of Mughal funerary architecture
• Mughal painting developed under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan
• Gardens, forts, mosques and mausoleums were major architectural forms

LITERATURE AND SOURCES

• Baburnama is an autobiographical source for Babur
• Akbarnama and Ain i Akbari by Abul Fazl are crucial for Akbar's reign
• Tuzuk i Jahangiri is an important source for Jahangir
• Court chronicles provide details of administration, economy and imperial ideology

DECLINE

• Weak successors after Aurangzeb could not maintain strong central authority
• Jagirdari crisis, factional struggles and financial pressure weakened the empire
• Regional powers such as Marathas, Sikhs, Jats and later autonomous Nawabs rose in strength
• Repeated invasions and internal fragmentation accelerated decline in the 18th century

SIGNIFICANCE

The Mughal Empire gave India a durable imperial framework, a sophisticated administrative structure, a major tradition of architecture and painting, and a powerful legacy in agrarian and revenue organization. Its institutions influenced later regional states and even colonial administration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Babur founded the empire in 1526 CE after the First Battle of Panipat
• Akbar was the real consolidator of Mughal rule
• Mansabdari was a rank system and Jagir was a revenue assignment
• Zabti and Dahsala are associated with Mughal revenue administration
• Jahangir is known for chain of justice and refined painting
• Shah Jahan is associated with architectural grandeur
• Aurangzeb expanded the empire most but also intensified strains of decline

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Mansab and Jagir. Mansab means rank while Jagir means revenue assignment. Sulh i kul is associated with Akbar, not Aurangzeb. Din i Ilahi was not a mass religion. Zabti is a revenue system, not a military arrangement.
Medieval History.Early Marathas:
INTRODUCTION

The rise of the Marathas in the 17th century marked a significant shift in Indian political history. Under Shivaji, the Marathas established a strong regional power that later challenged Mughal dominance and laid the foundation for a pan Indian empire.

BACKGROUND

• Decline of Deccan Sultanates and weakening of Mughal control in Deccan
• Harsh Mughal policies under Aurangzeb created resentment
• Geographical conditions of Western Ghats favored guerrilla warfare
• Rise of local warrior groups and leadership under Shivaji

SHIVAJI

• Founder of Maratha power
• Born in 1630 CE at Shivneri Fort
• Son of Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai
• Influenced by Bhakti saints and regional traditions
• Established independent kingdom through military skill and diplomacy

MILITARY SYSTEM

• Followed guerrilla warfare known as Ganimi Kava
• Strong network of forts for defense and control
• Efficient cavalry and light infantry
• Avoided large scale open battles
• Developed a navy to protect western coast

ADMINISTRATION

• Established a centralized administration
• Introduced Ashtapradhan council of eight ministers
• Key positions included Peshwa, Amatya, Sachiv, Senapati and others
• Efficient system of governance and record keeping

REVENUE SYSTEM

• Chauth was one fourth of revenue collected from territories
• Sardeshmukhi was an additional ten percent tax
• Land revenue formed main source of income
• Revenue collection was systematic and supervised

RELIGIOUS POLICY

• Followed policy of tolerance towards all religions
• Protected temples and respected local traditions
• Avoided unnecessary religious conflicts

EXPANSION

• Captured territories from Bijapur and Mughals
• Established control over large parts of Maharashtra
• Raids into Mughal territories weakened their control

SUCCESSORS

• Sambhaji succeeded Shivaji but faced Mughal opposition
• Rajaram continued resistance from southern forts
• Tarabai played important role in sustaining Maratha resistance

SIGNIFICANCE

• Established Maratha power as major political force
• Introduced effective military and administrative systems
• Laid foundation for later Maratha expansion across India
• Challenged Mughal supremacy in Deccan

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Shivaji is founder of Maratha power
• Ashtapradhan was council of ministers
• Guerrilla warfare was key military strategy
• Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were major taxes
• Forts played crucial role in defense

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Maratha revenue terms. Chauth was one fourth tax while Sardeshmukhi was an additional ten percent. Ashtapradhan was administrative council under Shivaji, not under Peshwas.

Modern History.Advent of Europeans:
ADVENT OF EUROPEANS IN INDIA

Introduction
• The advent of Europeans in India marked the beginning of a new phase in Indian history, eventually leading to colonial domination.
• The primary objective of Europeans was trade, especially in spices, textiles and luxury goods.
• Over time, commercial interests transformed into political and territorial control.

Background
• Renaissance in Europe increased curiosity and scientific temperament.
• Fall of Constantinople (1453) blocked traditional land trade routes to Asia.
• Rise of Mercantilism encouraged accumulation of bullion through trade.
• Need to bypass Arab intermediaries and Ottoman control.
• Advances in navigation (compass, astrolabe, cartography, shipbuilding).

PORTUGUESE

Introduction
• First Europeans to arrive in India.
• Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

Important Points
• Established first factory at Calicut.
• Followed policy of trade monopoly and naval dominance.
• Introduced Cartaz system (naval passes for trade).

Key Governors
• Francisco de Almeida – First Governor, followed ‘Blue Water Policy’ (naval supremacy).
• Alfonso de Albuquerque – Real founder of Portuguese power in India.

Features
• Captured Goa (1510) → became headquarters.
• Captured Malacca and Hormuz → control of trade routes.
• Introduced Christianity through missionaries.

Decline
• Weak successors after Albuquerque.
• Corruption and mismanagement.
• Rise of Dutch and English competition.
• Loss of naval supremacy.

PYQ Trap
• Blue Water Policy = Almeida (not Albuquerque).
• Goa captured in 1510 (frequently asked).

DUTCH

Introduction
• Dutch East India Company (VOC) established in 1602.

Important Points
• Focused mainly on spice trade (Indonesia priority).
• Established factories at Masulipatnam, Pulicat, Nagapattinam.

Features
• Strong naval power.
• Monopoly over spice trade in East Indies.

Decline
• Defeated by English in Battle of Bedara (1759).
• Shifted focus to Indonesia.

PYQ Trap
• Dutch decline in India due to English defeat, not Indian resistance.

ENGLISH

Introduction
• English East India Company established in 1600.
• Arrived for trade but later became political rulers.

Important Points
• First factory at Surat (1613).
• Sir Thomas Roe secured trade privileges from Jahangir.

Expansion
• Madras (Fort St George) – 1639
• Bombay – acquired from Portuguese (1661)
• Calcutta (Fort William) – 1690

Features
• Shift from trade to territorial control.
• Strong naval supremacy.
• Use of diplomacy and military power.

Significance
• Gradually emerged as dominant European power.
• Laid foundation of British Empire in India.

PYQ Trap
• First factory → Surat (not Madras).
• Bombay came from Portuguese dowry (Catherine of Braganza).

FRENCH

Introduction
• French East India Company established in 1664.

Important Points
• Main centres: Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe, Karaikal.

Features
• Strong political ambitions under Dupleix.
• Direct rivalry with English.

Carnatic Wars
• First Carnatic War (1746–48)
• Second Carnatic War (1749–54)
• Third Carnatic War (1758–63)

Outcome
• English victory → French political influence ended.

PYQ Trap
• Dupleix associated with French expansion.
• Carnatic Wars decided British supremacy.

DANISH

Introduction
• Danish East India Company established in 1616.

Important Points
• Settlements at Tranquebar and Serampore.

Features
• Limited political role.
• Focused mainly on trade and missionary activities.

Decline
• Sold settlements to British in 19th century.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Portuguese – First arrivals, early dominance.
• Dutch – Trade focused, lost to English.
• French – Political challenge, lost in Carnatic Wars.
• English – Most successful, established empire.

Significance
• Beginning of European colonialism in India.
• Integration of Indian economy with global trade.
• Shift from trade to territorial imperialism.
• Foundation of British rule.

PYQ Trap
• Sequence: Portuguese → Dutch → English → French → Danish.
• Only English succeeded in long-term political control.

Conclusion
• The advent of Europeans transformed India’s political and economic structure.
• What started as trade eventually resulted in colonial rule, with long-term consequences for India.
Modern History.British Conquests:
BRITISH CONQUESTS IN INDIA

Introduction
• British conquests in India marked the transition of the English East India Company from a trading entity to a territorial power.
• Through a combination of wars, diplomacy, alliances and administrative strategies, the British gradually established political dominance over India.

Background
• Decline of Mughal Empire after Aurangzeb created political fragmentation.
• Rise of regional powers like Marathas, Nawabs of Bengal, Mysore, Hyderabad.
• European rivalry, especially Anglo-French conflict, provided opportunity.
• Superior military organization, naval power and financial resources of British.

BATTLE OF PLASSEY (1757)

Introduction
• First major political victory of the British in India.
• Fought between Siraj-ud-Daulah and British led by Robert Clive.

Causes
• Misuse of trade privileges by British.
• Fortification of Calcutta without Nawab’s permission.
• Conspiracy with Mir Jafar and other nobles.

Features
• Treachery of Mir Jafar led to defeat of Siraj-ud-Daulah.
• British gained control over Bengal indirectly.

Significance
• Beginning of British political rule in India.
• Bengal’s vast resources came under British control.

PYQ Trap
• Plassey was not a full-scale battle, but largely a political conspiracy.

BATTLE OF BUXAR (1764)

Introduction
• Decisive battle establishing British supremacy in India.

Participants
• British vs combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II.

Features
• British victory due to superior military discipline.

Significance
• Treaty of Allahabad (1765).
• Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted to British.
• Beginning of dual government in Bengal.

PYQ Trap
• Buxar more decisive than Plassey in establishing British power.

ANGLO-MYSORE WARS

Introduction
• Series of four wars between British and Mysore rulers (Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan).

Important Points
• Hyder Ali emerged as strong opponent of British.
• Tipu Sultan modernized army and sought foreign alliances.

Outcome
• Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) – Tipu Sultan defeated and killed.
• Mysore reduced and brought under British control.

Significance
• End of major southern resistance.

PYQ Trap
• Tipu Sultan died in 1799 (Fourth Mysore War).

ANGLO-MARATHA WARS

Introduction
• Three wars fought between British and Marathas.

Important Points
• Maratha confederacy weakened due to internal rivalry.
• British used subsidiary alliance to divide powers.

Outcome
• Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) ended Maratha power.
• Peshwa abolished.

Significance
• British became supreme power in India.

PYQ Trap
• Final defeat of Marathas in 1818.

ANGLO-SIKH WARS

Introduction
• Two wars fought between British and Sikh Empire.

Features
• Strong army built by Ranjit Singh.
• After his death, political instability weakened Sikhs.

Outcome
• Second Anglo-Sikh War (1849) → Punjab annexed.

Significance
• Last major kingdom annexed before 1857.

PYQ Trap
• Punjab annexed in 1849.

EXPANSION POLICIES

SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE

Introduction
• Introduced by Lord Wellesley.

Features
• Indian rulers had to accept British troops.
• Payment for maintenance of troops.
• No independent foreign relations.

Significance
• Reduced Indian rulers to dependent status.

DOCTRINE OF LAPSE

Introduction
• Introduced by Lord Dalhousie.

Features
• States without natural heirs annexed by British.

Examples
• Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur.

PYQ Trap
• Jhansi annexed under Doctrine of Lapse.

DIRECT ANNEXATIONS

Important Points
• Awadh annexed in 1856 on grounds of misgovernance.

Significance
• Created widespread resentment leading to Revolt of 1857.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Early phase → military conquest (Plassey, Buxar).
• Middle phase → wars (Mysore, Maratha, Sikh).
• Later phase → policies (Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse).

Significance
• British established political supremacy over India.
• Indian states lost sovereignty gradually.

PYQ Trap
• Expansion was combination of war + diplomacy + policy.

Conclusion
• British conquests were systematic and strategic.
• By mid-19th century, most of India came under British control, paving the way for colonial rule.
Modern History.Administrative Policies of British:
ADMINISTRATIVE POLICIES OF THE BRITISH IN INDIA

Introduction
• The British introduced a centralized and structured administrative system in India to consolidate their political control.
• Their administrative policies aimed at efficient revenue collection, maintenance of law and order, and strengthening colonial rule.
• These policies transformed traditional Indian governance and laid the foundation of modern administration.

Background
• Decline of Mughal administration created a vacuum.
• Need for systematic governance after territorial expansion.
• Influence of British parliamentary system and utilitarian ideas.

CENTRAL ADMINISTRATION

Regulating Act 1773
• First step by British Parliament to control East India Company.
• Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal.
• Warren Hastings became first Governor-General.
• Established Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774).

Pitt’s India Act 1784
• Introduced dual control – Company + British Government.
• Board of Control established.
• Reduced Company autonomy.

Charter Acts
• Charter Act 1813 – End of trade monopoly (except tea and China trade).
• Charter Act 1833 – Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck).
• Charter Act 1853 – Introduced open competition for civil services.

PYQ Trap
• 1833 Act centralized administration completely.

CIVIL SERVICES

Introduction
• Civil services became backbone of British administration.

Features
• Initially dominated by Europeans.
• Recruitment through competitive exams (after 1853).
• ICS (Indian Civil Service) became elite service.

Significance
• Ensured efficient administration.
• Strengthened British control over vast territories.

PYQ Trap
• ICS exam initially held only in London.

JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION

Introduction
• British introduced modern judicial system.

Features
• Establishment of Supreme Court (1774).
• Introduction of codified laws.
• Separation of judiciary from executive (gradually).

Important Reforms
• Cornwallis Code (1793) – judicial reforms.
• Establishment of civil and criminal courts.

Significance
• Uniform legal system across India.

PYQ Trap
• Cornwallis known as ‘Father of Civil Services in India’.

POLICE ADMINISTRATION

Introduction
• Organized police system introduced for maintaining law and order.

Features
• Cornwallis introduced modern police system.
• District divided into police stations (thanas).
• Daroga system introduced.

Significance
• Strengthened internal security.
• Helped in suppression of revolts.

REVENUE ADMINISTRATION

Introduction
• Revenue was primary objective of British rule.

Systems
• Permanent Settlement (1793) – Bengal (Zamindari system).
• Ryotwari System – Madras and Bombay (direct settlement with peasants).
• Mahalwari System – North India (village-based system).

Significance
• Maximized revenue extraction.
• Disrupted traditional agrarian relations.

PYQ Trap
• Permanent Settlement introduced by Lord Cornwallis.

LOCAL ADMINISTRATION

Introduction
• Development of local governance structures.

Features
• Lord Ripon – Father of Local Self Government.
• Introduction of municipalities and local boards.

Significance
• Beginning of decentralization.
• Training ground for Indian leadership.

PYQ Trap
• Lord Ripon associated with local self-government (not Curzon).

MILITARY ADMINISTRATION

Introduction
• Strong military organization ensured British dominance.

Features
• Modern army with European training.
• Use of Indian sepoys under British officers.
• Divide and rule policy in recruitment.

Significance
• Helped in expansion and control of empire.

COMMUNICATION ADMINISTRATION

Important Points
• Introduction of railways (1853).
• Telegraph system introduced.
• Postal system expanded.

Significance
• Improved administrative efficiency.
• Facilitated control over distant regions.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Centralized system replaced traditional decentralized structures.
• Focus shifted from welfare to revenue and control.

Significance
• Foundation of modern administrative system in India.
• Legacy continues in present governance structure.

PYQ Trap
• British administration = centralized + bureaucratic.

Conclusion
• British administrative policies were designed to strengthen colonial rule.
• While exploitative in nature, they introduced institutions that later evolved into modern Indian administration.
Modern History.Social Policies of British:
SOCIAL POLICIES OF THE BRITISH IN INDIA

Introduction
• The British introduced several social policies in India, partly influenced by humanitarian ideals and partly to strengthen colonial control.
• These policies aimed at reforming Indian society but also led to cultural changes and resistance.

Background
• Influence of Enlightenment ideas, liberalism and utilitarian philosophy.
• Pressure from Christian missionaries and social reformers.
• Need to create a class of Indians loyal to British rule.

ABOLITION OF SOCIAL EVILS

Sati Abolition
• Sati system abolished in 1829 by Lord William Bentinck.
• Strongly supported by Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

Female Infanticide
• Declared illegal and measures taken to prevent it.

Thuggee Suppression
• Organized suppression of Thuggee under William Sleeman.

Significance
• Marked beginning of state intervention in social customs.

PYQ Trap
• Sati abolished in 1829 (not 1833 or later).

WIDOW REMARRIAGE AND WOMEN REFORMS

Widow Remarriage Act 1856
• Legalized remarriage of Hindu widows.
• Supported by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

Other Measures
• Efforts to improve condition of women.
• Promotion of female education.

Significance
• Beginning of women empowerment in modern India.

PYQ Trap
• Vidyasagar associated with Widow Remarriage Act.

EDUCATION POLICY

Introduction
• Education used as tool for social and administrative transformation.

Important Developments
• Macaulay’s Minute (1835) – promotion of English education.
• Wood’s Despatch (1854) – blueprint of modern education system.

Features
• Emphasis on Western education and English language.
• Downward Filtration Theory – educating upper class to influence masses.

Significance
• Creation of educated middle class.
• Spread of modern ideas like liberty, equality.

PYQ Trap
• Wood’s Despatch called ‘Magna Carta of English Education in India’.

MISSIONARY ACTIVITIES

Introduction
• Christian missionaries played key role in social reforms.

Features
• Spread of education and healthcare.
• Criticism of Indian social practices.

Impact
• Led to reform movements within Indian society.

PYQ Trap
• Missionaries promoted Western education alongside religion.

SOCIAL LEGISLATIONS

Important Laws
• Age of Consent Act 1891.
• Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 (later development).

Features
• Regulated social practices.
• Attempt to modernize society.

Significance
• Increased state role in social matters.

RACIAL POLICIES

Introduction
• British followed racial discrimination despite reforms.

Features
• Indians excluded from higher administrative positions.
• Segregation in social and public life.

Impact
• Created resentment among Indians.

PYQ Trap
• British reforms were not purely humanitarian; they had political motives.

IMPACT ON INDIAN SOCIETY

Positive Effects
• Abolition of harmful practices.
• Spread of education and modern ideas.

Negative Effects
• Cultural alienation.
• Social tensions and resistance.

Significance
• Rise of socio-religious reform movements.
• Growth of nationalism.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Early phase – reform oriented (Bentinck period).
• Later phase – cautious approach due to resistance (post-1857).

PYQ Trap
• Post-1857 British avoided aggressive social reforms.

Conclusion
• British social policies had mixed impact.
• While they introduced progressive reforms, their underlying objective remained strengthening colonial rule.
Modern History.Economic Policies of British:
ECONOMIC POLICIES OF THE BRITISH IN INDIA

Introduction
• The British economic policies in India were primarily aimed at maximizing profits for Britain.
• These policies led to systematic exploitation of Indian resources and deindustrialization of traditional economy.
• India was transformed into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods.

Background
• Influence of Mercantilism in early phase.
• Later shift to Free Trade policy after Industrial Revolution in Britain.
• Need for raw materials and markets for British industries.

LAND REVENUE SYSTEMS

Permanent Settlement (1793)
• Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal.
• Zamindars made owners of land and responsible for revenue collection.
• Fixed revenue demand.

Impact
• Creation of absentee landlordism.
• Exploitation of peasants.

Ryotwari System
• Introduced by Thomas Munro in Madras and Bombay.
• Direct settlement with peasants (ryots).

Impact
• High revenue demand burdened peasants.
• Increased indebtedness.

Mahalwari System
• Introduced by Holt Mackenzie.
• Settlement with village communities.

Impact
• Collective responsibility increased pressure on villages.

PYQ Trap
• Permanent Settlement → Cornwallis; Ryotwari → Munro.

DEINDUSTRIALIZATION

Introduction
• Decline of traditional handicrafts and industries.

Causes
• Import of cheap machine-made goods from Britain.
• Loss of patronage after decline of Indian rulers.
• Discriminatory tariff policies.

Impact
• Collapse of textile industry.
• Rise of unemployment among artisans.

PYQ Trap
• India became exporter of raw materials, importer of finished goods.

DRAIN OF WEALTH

Introduction
• Concept explained by Dadabhai Naoroji.

Features
• Unrequited transfer of wealth from India to Britain.
• Payments for salaries, pensions, profits, and administrative expenses.

Impact
• Continuous economic drain weakened Indian economy.

Significance
• Became major economic critique of British rule.

PYQ Trap
• Dadabhai Naoroji → Drain Theory.

COMMERCIALIZATION OF AGRICULTURE

Introduction
• Shift from subsistence farming to commercial crops.

Features
• Cultivation of cash crops like indigo, cotton, jute.
• Farmers forced to grow crops for export.

Impact
• Food shortages and famines.
• Increased vulnerability of peasants.

PYQ Trap
• Indigo cultivation linked with exploitation (Indigo Revolt).

INDUSTRIAL POLICIES

Introduction
• British policies discouraged Indian industrial growth.

Features
• Lack of support to Indian industries.
• Focus on British industrial interests.

Impact
• India remained underdeveloped industrially.

RAILWAYS AND INFRASTRUCTURE

Introduction
• Railways introduced in 1853.

Features
• Built primarily for economic exploitation.
• Facilitated movement of raw materials to ports.

Impact
• Integrated markets but benefited British economy.

PYQ Trap
• Railways served colonial interests first, not Indian development.

TRADE POLICIES

Introduction
• Shift from mercantilism to free trade.

Features
• Removal of trade barriers for British goods.
• Imposition of heavy duties on Indian goods in Britain.

Impact
• India became dependent on British economy.

FAMINES AND ECONOMIC IMPACT

Introduction
• Frequent famines during British rule.

Causes
• Revenue policies and commercialization.
• Neglect of agriculture and irrigation.

Impact
• Massive loss of life.
• Exposure of colonial exploitation.

PYQ Trap
• Famines linked to economic policies, not just natural causes.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Early phase – Mercantilist exploitation.
• Later phase – Free trade exploitation.

Significance
• Transformation of Indian economy into colonial economy.

IMPACT ON INDIA

Positive Effects
• Development of transport and communication.

Negative Effects
• Deindustrialization.
• Poverty and unemployment.
• Economic dependency.

Conclusion
• British economic policies were exploitative in nature.
• They led to long-term structural changes that adversely affected India’s economy and contributed to widespread poverty.
Modern History.Revolt of 1857:
REVOLT OF 1857

Introduction
• The Revolt of 1857 was the first major uprising against British rule in India.
• It began as a sepoy mutiny but soon turned into a widespread revolt involving various sections of society.
• It is also referred to as the First War of Independence by some historians.

Nature of the Revolt
• Sepoy Mutiny – started among soldiers of the East India Company.
• Civil Rebellion – participation of peasants, zamindars and rulers in many regions.
• Regional Revolt – limited geographical spread, mainly in North and Central India.

Background
• Political annexations under Doctrine of Lapse.
• Economic exploitation and heavy land revenue demands.
• Social and religious interference by British.
• Discontent among soldiers due to discrimination.

Causes

Political Causes
• Annexation of states like Jhansi, Satara and Nagpur.
• Annexation of Awadh (1856) on grounds of misgovernance.
• Displacement of traditional rulers and elites.

Economic Causes
• Heavy land revenue systems.
• Decline of handicrafts and traditional industries.
• Exploitation of peasants and artisans.

Social and Religious Causes
• Fear of conversion to Christianity.
• Abolition of social practices like Sati created suspicion.
• Introduction of Western education.

Military Causes
• Discrimination in pay and promotion.
• General Service Enlistment Act (1856) offended religious sentiments.
• Use of Enfield rifle cartridges greased with cow and pig fat.

Immediate Cause
• Refusal of sepoys to use greased cartridges.
• Incident at Barrackpore and Meerut triggered the revolt.

Course of the Revolt

Major Centres
• Meerut – starting point (May 1857).
• Delhi – Bahadur Shah II declared as leader.
• Kanpur – Nana Saheb.
• Jhansi – Rani Lakshmibai.
• Lucknow – Begum Hazrat Mahal.
• Bihar – Kunwar Singh.

Features
• Rapid spread across North India.
• Participation of different social groups.

Suppression
• British used superior military strength.
• Lack of coordination among rebels.
• By 1858, revolt was suppressed.

PYQ Trap
• Revolt began at Meerut, not Barrackpore.

Causes of Failure

Political
• Lack of unified leadership.
• Limited support from princely states.

Military
• Inferior weapons and organization.
• Lack of modern communication.

Social
• No participation from all sections of society.
• Southern and eastern India largely remained unaffected.

PYQ Trap
• Revolt was not pan-India in nature.

Consequences

Administrative Changes
• End of East India Company rule (1858).
• Transfer of power to British Crown.

Policy Changes
• End of Doctrine of Lapse.
• Assurance to princes regarding their territories.

Military Reforms
• Reorganization of army.
• Increase in proportion of European soldiers.

Social Policy Changes
• British adopted non-interference in social and religious matters.

Significance
• First major challenge to British rule.
• Beginning of organized resistance.
• Exposed weaknesses of colonial rule.

Historiographical Debate
• British view – Sepoy Mutiny.
• Indian nationalists – First War of Independence.
• Modern view – combination of both.

PYQ Trap
• Nature of revolt = mixed (not purely national, not purely mutiny).

Conclusion
• The Revolt of 1857 marked a turning point in Indian history.
• Though it failed, it laid the foundation for future national movements and exposed the exploitative nature of British rule.
Modern History.Peasant Movements:
PEASANT MOVEMENTS IN INDIA

Introduction
• Peasant movements in India emerged as a response to oppressive land revenue systems, exploitation by landlords, moneylenders and colonial policies.
• These movements reflected agrarian distress and resistance against economic exploitation under British rule.

Background
• Introduction of exploitative land revenue systems.
• Commercialization of agriculture.
• Rise of intermediaries like zamindars and moneylenders.
• Frequent famines and indebtedness of peasants.

INDIGO REVOLT (1859–60)

Introduction
• First major peasant movement against British planters.

Causes
• Forced cultivation of indigo under oppressive conditions.
• Low prices and high exploitation by European planters.

Features
• Peasants refused to grow indigo.
• Support from intelligentsia and press.

Outcome
• Indigo cultivation declined.
• Indigo Commission appointed.

PYQ Trap
• Indigo revolt associated with Bengal.

DECCAN RIOTS (1875)

Introduction
• Occurred in Poona and Ahmednagar regions.

Causes
• Heavy indebtedness of peasants.
• Exploitation by moneylenders (sahukars).

Features
• Attacks on moneylenders.
• Burning of debt records.

Outcome
• Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act (1879).

PYQ Trap
• Target of peasants = moneylenders, not British directly.

PABNA AGRARIAN UNREST (1870s)

Introduction
• Movement in Bengal against zamindars.

Causes
• Illegal rent enhancement.
• Exploitation by landlords.

Features
• Peaceful resistance.
• Formation of agrarian leagues.

Outcome
• Tenancy reforms initiated.

PYQ Trap
• Pabna movement was largely non-violent.

CHAMPARAN SATYAGRAHA (1917)

Introduction
• First major Gandhian peasant movement.

Causes
• Tinkathia system forcing indigo cultivation.
• Exploitation by European planters.

Features
• Gandhi used satyagraha method.
• Involvement of local peasants.

Outcome
• Abolition of Tinkathia system.

PYQ Trap
• First experiment of Gandhi in India.

KHEDA SATYAGRAHA (1918)

Introduction
• Peasant movement in Gujarat led by Gandhi.

Causes
• Crop failure and demand for tax remission.

Features
• Non-payment of revenue by peasants.

Outcome
• Suspension of revenue collection.

BARDOLI SATYAGRAHA (1928)

Introduction
• Led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Causes
• Increase in land revenue by 30%.

Features
• Organized and disciplined movement.

Outcome
• Government withdrew revenue hike.

PYQ Trap
• Patel got title ‘Sardar’ after Bardoli movement.

TEBHAGA MOVEMENT (1946–47)

Introduction
• Movement in Bengal by sharecroppers.

Causes
• Demand for two-thirds share of produce.

Features
• Organized by Kisan Sabha.

Outcome
• Partial success and later reforms.

TELANGANA MOVEMENT (1946–51)

Introduction
• Peasant uprising in Hyderabad State.

Causes
• Feudal oppression by landlords.

Features
• Armed struggle.

Outcome
• Suppressed but influenced land reforms.

PYQ Trap
• Telangana movement had militant character.

COMMON FEATURES

Important Points
• Reaction against economic exploitation.
• Participation of peasants and tenants.
• Varied methods – violent and non-violent.

Significance
• Exposed agrarian distress under colonial rule.
• Contributed to national movement.
• Led to agrarian reforms in later period.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Early movements – localized and spontaneous.
• Later movements – organized and politically guided.

Conclusion
• Peasant movements were an important aspect of resistance against British policies.
• They played a crucial role in shaping agrarian consciousness and strengthening the freedom struggle.
Modern History.Tribal Revolts:
TRIBAL REVOLTS IN INDIA

Introduction
• Tribal revolts were uprisings by indigenous communities against British policies and exploitation.
• These revolts were a reaction to loss of traditional rights over land, forests and resources.
• They were often localized but reflected deep resistance to colonial intrusion.

Background
• British land revenue policies disrupted traditional tribal systems.
• Introduction of private property in land.
• Encroachment of forests by outsiders (dikus).
• Exploitation by moneylenders, landlords and contractors.

SANTRAL (SANTHAL) REVOLT (1855–56)

Introduction
• One of the largest tribal uprisings.

Causes
• Exploitation by zamindars and moneylenders.
• Loss of land and indebtedness.

Leaders
• Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu.

Features
• Organized mass uprising.
• Attacks on British officials and moneylenders.

Outcome
• Suppressed by British.
• Creation of Santhal Pargana.

PYQ Trap
• Leaders – Sidhu and Kanhu (frequently asked).

MUNDA REVOLT (ULGULAN) (1899–1900)

Introduction
• Led by Birsa Munda.

Causes
• Alienation of tribal land.
• Forced labour and exploitation.

Features
• Religious and political movement.
• Demand for restoration of traditional rights.

Outcome
• Suppressed but led to reforms.

PYQ Trap
• Birsa Munda associated with ‘Ulgulan’ (Great Tumult).

KHOND REVOLT

Introduction
• Revolt in Odisha region.

Causes
• British interference in tribal customs.
• Suppression of human sacrifice (Meriah system).

Features
• Resistance against colonial intrusion.

Outcome
• Gradual suppression.

BHIL REVOLTS

Introduction
• Occurred in Western India.

Causes
• Loss of traditional rights.
• Economic exploitation.

Features
• Frequent uprisings.

Outcome
• Eventually suppressed.

KOL REVOLT (1831–32)

Introduction
• Revolt in Chotanagpur region.

Causes
• Land alienation and exploitation by outsiders.

Features
• Violent uprising.

Outcome
• Suppressed by British forces.

PYQ Trap
• Kol revolt one of the earliest tribal uprisings.

RAMPA REVOLT (1922–24)

Introduction
• Led by Alluri Sitarama Raju in Andhra region.

Causes
• Restrictions on forest use.
• Forced labour.

Features
• Guerrilla warfare tactics.

Outcome
• Suppressed after Raju’s death.

PYQ Trap
• Alluri Sitarama Raju associated with Rampa revolt.

KHASI AND GARO REVOLTS

Introduction
• Revolts in North-East India.

Causes
• British interference and road construction.

Features
• Resistance led by tribal chiefs.

Outcome
• Suppressed.

COMMON FEATURES

Important Points
• Reaction against exploitation and land alienation.
• Resistance against forest policies.
• Led by tribal leaders.

Significance
• Highlighted tribal grievances.
• Forced British to introduce protective laws.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Early revolts – spontaneous and localized.
• Later revolts – more organized and political.

PYQ Trap
• Tribal revolts were mainly local, not pan-India movements.

Conclusion
• Tribal revolts were an important form of resistance against colonial rule.
• They reflected the struggle of tribal communities to protect their identity, land and autonomy.
Modern History.Caste Movements:
CASTE MOVEMENTS IN MODERN INDIA

Introduction
• Caste movements in modern India emerged as a response to social inequalities, discrimination and rigid caste hierarchy.
• These movements aimed at social reform, upliftment of lower castes and challenging Brahmanical dominance.
• They played a crucial role in shaping modern Indian society and politics.

Background
• Rigid caste system with social and economic discrimination.
• Denial of education, temple entry and social mobility to lower castes.
• Impact of Western education and ideas of equality and liberty.

EARLY ANTI-CASTE MOVEMENTS

Jyotiba Phule Movement

Introduction
• Led by Jyotirao Phule in Maharashtra.

Causes
• Oppression of lower castes by Brahmanical order.

Features
• Founded Satyashodhak Samaj (1873).
• Emphasis on education and social equality.

Outcome
• Spread awareness among backward classes.

PYQ Trap
• Satyashodhak Samaj → Phule (frequently asked).

Sri Narayana Guru Movement

Introduction
• Movement in Kerala against caste discrimination.

Features
• Promoted social equality.
• Established temples open to all castes.

Slogan
• “One caste, one religion, one God for mankind.”

SELF-RESPECT MOVEMENT

Introduction
• Led by E.V. Ramasamy Naicker (Periyar) in Tamil Nadu.

Causes
• Opposition to Brahmanical dominance.

Features
• Promotion of rationalism.
• Opposition to caste hierarchy and social inequality.

Outcome
• Strengthened anti-caste ideology.

PYQ Trap
• Self-Respect Movement → Periyar.

DALIT MOVEMENTS

Introduction
• Focus on upliftment of untouchables (Dalits).

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Movement

Features
• Advocacy for rights of Dalits.
• Demand for separate electorates.
• Role in drafting Constitution.

Important Events
• Mahad Satyagraha (1927) – right to access public water.
• Temple entry movements.

Outcome
• Legal and constitutional safeguards for Dalits.

PYQ Trap
• Ambedkar associated with Mahad Satyagraha.

Temple Entry Movements

Introduction
• Movements for entry of lower castes into temples.

Examples
• Vaikom Satyagraha (Kerala).

Outcome
• Gradual removal of caste barriers.

NON-BRAHMIN MOVEMENTS

Introduction
• Movements against Brahmin dominance in administration and education.

Features
• Demand for reservations and representation.

Example
• Justice Party in Madras Presidency.

PYQ Trap
• Justice Party → Non-Brahmin movement.

COMMON FEATURES

Important Points
• Challenge to caste hierarchy.
• Emphasis on social equality and education.
• Leadership by social reformers.

Significance
• Led to social reforms.
• Influenced nationalist movement.
• Foundation for affirmative action policies.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Regional variations in caste movements.
• Some movements were reformist, others radical.

Conclusion
• Caste movements played a transformative role in Indian society.
• They helped in reducing caste-based inequalities and laid the foundation for a more egalitarian society.
Modern History.Socio-Religious Reform Movements:
SOCIO-RELIGIOUS REFORM MOVEMENTS IN MODERN INDIA

Introduction
• Socio-religious reform movements emerged in the 19th century to address social evils, religious superstitions and rigid traditions in Indian society.
• They were influenced by Western education, rationalism and humanitarian ideas.
• These movements aimed at reforming society and reviving the ethical foundations of religion.

Background
• Spread of Western education and modern ideas.
• Impact of Christian missionaries.
• Social evils like sati, child marriage, caste discrimination and illiteracy.
• Rise of a new educated middle class.

BRAHMO SAMAJ

Introduction
• Founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828.

Features
• Monotheism.
• Opposition to idol worship and caste system.
• Promotion of women’s rights and education.

Reforms
• Abolition of sati.
• Advocacy for widow remarriage.

PYQ Trap

ARYA SAMAJ

Introduction
• Founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in 1875.

Features
• Back to the Vedas.

Reforms

• Promotion of women’s education.

PYQ Trap

PRARTHANA SAMAJ

Introduction
• Founded by Atmaram Pandurang.

Features
• Inspired by Brahmo Samaj.
• Emphasis on social reforms.

Reforms
• Widow remarriage.
• Female education.

RAMAKRISHNA MISSION

Introduction
• Founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897.

Features
• Practical Vedanta.
• Service to humanity.

Activities
• Education and social service.

ALIGARH MOVEMENT

Introduction
• Led by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.

Features

• Establishment of Aligarh College.

• Modernization of Muslim society.

THEOSOPHICAL MOVEMENT

Introduction
• Led by Annie Besant.

Features

YOUNG BENGAL MOVEMENT

Introduction
• Led by Henry Vivian Derozio.

Features

DEOBAND MOVEMENT

Introduction
• Founded by Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi.

Features

SINGH SABHA MOVEMENT

Introduction
• Reform movement among Sikhs.

Features
• Revival of Sikh identity.
• Removal of superstitions.

COMMON FEATURES

Important Points
• Opposition to social evils.
• Emphasis on education and rationalism.
• Religious reform combined with social change.

Differences
• Reformist vs revivalist movements.
• Western-oriented vs traditional approaches.

Significance
• Led to social transformation.
• Prepared ground for national movement.
• Promoted modern values of equality and justice.

PYQ Trap
• Reform movements = mix of reform + revival (not purely one).

Conclusion
• Socio-religious reform movements played a crucial role in modernizing Indian society.
• They laid the foundation for social awakening and contributed to the growth of nationalism.
Modern History.Moderate Phase (1885–1905):
MODERATE PHASE OF INDIAN NATIONAL MOVEMENT (1885–1905)

Introduction
• The Moderate Phase marks the early stage of the Indian National Movement from 1885 to 1905.
• It was led by early leaders of the Indian National Congress who believed in constitutional methods and dialogue with the British.
• Their approach was gradual reform rather than immediate independence.

Background
• Formation of Indian National Congress in 1885.
• Rise of educated middle class.
• Influence of Western liberal ideas like democracy and rights.

Leaders
• Dadabhai Naoroji
• Gopal Krishna Gokhale
• Surendranath Banerjee
• Pherozeshah Mehta

PYQ Trap
• Dadabhai Naoroji → Drain Theory (frequently linked with Moderates).

Ideology

Features
• Faith in British justice and fairness.
• Belief in constitutional and peaceful methods.
• Demand for gradual reforms.

Methods

Important Points
• Petitions and resolutions.
• Memorandums to British authorities.
• Participation in legislative councils.

PYQ Trap
• Moderates followed ‘3Ps’ → Prayer, Petition, Protest.

Demands

Political Demands
• Expansion of legislative councils.
• Greater Indian representation in administration.

Economic Demands
• Reduction of land revenue.
• Criticism of economic drain.

Administrative Demands
• Indianization of civil services.
• Separation of judiciary and executive.

Economic Critique

Introduction
• Moderates exposed economic exploitation of British rule.

Features
• Drain of wealth theory.
• Criticism of high taxation.

Significance
• Created economic awareness among Indians.

Achievements

Important Points
• Spread of political awareness.
• Creation of nationalist consciousness.
• Formation of a political platform (INC).

Limitations

Political
• Limited mass participation.
• Elite leadership.

Ideological
• Excessive faith in British intentions.

Outcome
• Failure to achieve major political reforms.

PYQ Trap
• Moderates were not mass leaders; mainly elite-based.

Decline

Causes
• Frustration over slow progress.
• Rise of assertive leaders (Extremists).
• Partition of Bengal (1905) intensified opposition.

Transition
• Led to emergence of Extremist Phase.

Significance

Important Points
• Laid foundation of national movement.
• Introduced political methods and ideas.
• Created awareness of rights and governance.

Conclusion
• Though limited in achievements, the Moderates played a crucial role in initiating organized political activity in India.
• They laid the groundwork for future phases of the freedom struggle.
Modern History.Extremist Phase (1905–1917):
EXTREMIST PHASE OF INDIAN NATIONAL MOVEMENT (1905–1917)

Introduction
• The Extremist Phase marked a radical shift in the Indian National Movement between 1905 and 1917.
• It emerged due to dissatisfaction with the moderate approach and aimed at achieving Swaraj through assertive methods.
• Leaders of this phase emphasized self-reliance, mass participation and direct action.

Background
• Failure of moderate methods to achieve significant reforms.
• Growing economic exploitation and political discontent.
• Partition of Bengal in 1905 acted as a major trigger.

Leaders
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak
• Bipin Chandra Pal
• Lala Lajpat Rai

PYQ Trap
• Lal-Bal-Pal → core extremist leadership.

Ideology

Features
• Swaraj as the ultimate goal.
• Rejection of faith in British justice.
• Emphasis on self-reliance and nationalism.

Methods

Important Points
• Swadeshi movement (use of indigenous goods).
• Boycott of foreign goods.
• National education movement.
• Passive resistance and mass mobilization.

PYQ Trap
• Swadeshi + Boycott → key extremist tools.

Partition of Bengal (1905)

Introduction
• Division of Bengal by Lord Curzon.

Impact
• Sparked mass protests.
• Led to rise of extremist nationalism.

Features of Movement
• Public meetings and processions.
• Use of symbols like Vande Mataram.

PYQ Trap
• Partition of Bengal → major turning point.

Achievements

Important Points
• Expansion of national movement beyond elites.
• Rise of mass participation.
• Strengthening of nationalist sentiment.

Limitations

Political
• Lack of unified strategy.
• Internal differences within Congress.

Organizational
• Weak coordination among leaders.

Outcome
• Surat Split (1907) between Moderates and Extremists.

PYQ Trap
• Surat Split → 1907 (frequently asked).

Decline

Causes
• Government repression.
• Arrest of leaders like Tilak.
• Internal conflicts.

Transition
• Led to emergence of revolutionary activities and later Gandhian phase.

Significance

Important Points
• Shift from elite politics to mass politics.
• Promotion of national pride and self-reliance.
• Prepared ground for future movements.

Conclusion
• The Extremist Phase marked a decisive transformation in the freedom struggle.
• It infused new energy into the movement and laid the foundation for mass-based nationalism in India.
Modern History.Swadeshi Movement:
SWADESHI MOVEMENT (1905–1908)

Introduction
• The Swadeshi Movement was one of the most important mass movements in the Indian National Movement.
• It began as a reaction to the Partition of Bengal in 1905 by Lord Curzon.
• It emphasized the use of indigenous goods and boycott of foreign products.

Background
• Partition of Bengal aimed at dividing and weakening nationalist unity.
• Growing dissatisfaction with British policies.
• Rise of extremist leaders advocating assertive nationalism.

Objectives

Important Points
• Promotion of Swadeshi (use of indigenous goods).
• Boycott of foreign goods.
• Development of national education.
• Strengthening of Indian industries.

Methods

Features
• Boycott of British goods, especially textiles.
• Promotion of indigenous industries and products.
• Establishment of national schools and colleges.
• Public meetings, processions and bonfires of foreign goods.

PYQ Trap
• Swadeshi ≠ only boycott; includes promotion of indigenous industry.

Spread of Movement

Important Points
• Bengal was the center.
• Spread to Maharashtra, Punjab and Madras.
• Participation of students, women and middle class.

Leadership

Leaders
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak
• Bipin Chandra Pal
• Lala Lajpat Rai
• Aurobindo Ghosh

PYQ Trap
• Aurobindo Ghosh → ideological leader of Swadeshi.

Role of Education

Introduction
• National education movement emerged.

Features
• Establishment of institutions independent of British control.
• Emphasis on Indian values and culture.

Economic Impact

Important Points
• Growth of indigenous industries.
• Decline in import of British goods.

Social Impact

Important Points
• Rise of nationalism among masses.
• Participation of women and youth.

Limitations

Political
• Limited to urban areas.
• Lack of participation from peasants and workers.

Organizational
• Absence of strong central leadership.

Decline

Causes
• Repression by British government.
• Arrest of leaders.
• Surat Split (1907) weakened unity.

PYQ Trap
• Movement declined after Surat Split and repression.

Significance

Important Points
• First major mass movement of 20th century.
• Shift towards assertive nationalism.
• Promotion of economic nationalism.

Conclusion
• The Swadeshi Movement marked a turning point in the Indian freedom struggle.
• It introduced new methods of protest and laid the foundation for future mass movements.
Modern History.Lucknow Session of INC (1916):
LUCKNOW SESSION OF INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS (1916)

Introduction
• The Lucknow Session of the Indian National Congress was held in 1916.
• It is significant for the reunion of Moderates and Extremists and the agreement between Congress and the Muslim League.

Background
• Split between Moderates and Extremists at Surat (1907).
• Growing need for unity in the national movement.
• Rise of nationalist sentiment during World War I.

Reunion of Congress

Introduction
• Moderates and Extremists reunited after nearly a decade.

Significance
• Strengthened the national movement.
• Created a united political front against British rule.

PYQ Trap
• Reunion after Surat Split → Lucknow Session 1916.

Lucknow Pact (1916)

Introduction
• Agreement between Indian National Congress and All India Muslim League.

Features
• Joint demands for constitutional reforms.
• Acceptance of separate electorates for Muslims by Congress.
• Agreement on representation of different communities.

Significance
• Marked Hindu-Muslim unity.
• Strengthened demand for self-government.

PYQ Trap
• Congress accepted separate electorates (important prelim point).

Leaders Involved

Important Personalities
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak
• Annie Besant
• Muhammad Ali Jinnah (member of both Congress and League at that time)

PYQ Trap
• Jinnah called “Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity”.

Importance

Political Impact
• Strengthened unity within Congress.
• Enhanced cooperation between Congress and Muslim League.

Strategic Impact
• Increased pressure on British government for reforms.

Limitations

Important Points
• Separate electorates later contributed to communal divisions.
• Unity was temporary.

Conclusion
• The Lucknow Session of 1916 was a milestone in the Indian National Movement.
• It symbolized unity and cooperation but also laid the groundwork for future political challenges.
Modern History.Home Rule Movement:
HOME RULE MOVEMENT (1916–1918)

Introduction
• The Home Rule Movement was launched in 1916 to demand self-government (Home Rule) for India within the British Empire.
• It marked the revival of the national movement after the decline of the Extremist phase.
• The movement aimed to generate political awareness and mobilize public opinion.

Background
• Decline of nationalist activity after 1908 due to repression.
• Impact of World War I and rising political expectations.
• Need for a more organized and widespread movement.

Leaders

Important Personalities
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak
• Annie Besant

PYQ Trap
• Tilak and Annie Besant → key leaders of Home Rule Movement.

Home Rule Leagues

Tilak’s League
• Established in April 1916.
• Operated in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Provinces and Berar.

Annie Besant’s League
• Established in September 1916.
• Operated in rest of India including Madras.

PYQ Trap
• Two leagues with separate areas of operation.

Objectives

Important Points
• Self-government within British Empire.
• Promotion of political awareness.
• Expansion of nationalist movement.

Methods

Features
• Public meetings and lectures.
• Distribution of pamphlets and newspapers.
• Mobilization of educated middle class.

PYQ Trap
• Movement was constitutional, not revolutionary.

Role of Press

Introduction
• Newspapers played a key role.

Examples
• Tilak’s ‘Kesari’.
• Annie Besant’s ‘New India’.

Significance

Political Impact
• Revived national movement.
• Prepared ground for Gandhian mass movements.

Social Impact
• Increased political awareness among Indians.

Limitations

Important Points
• Limited mass participation (mainly middle class).
• Lack of unified leadership.

Decline

Causes
• Government repression.
• Arrest of Annie Besant.
• Montagu Declaration (1917) promising reforms.

PYQ Trap
• Montagu Declaration weakened the movement.

Conclusion
• The Home Rule Movement was an important step in India’s struggle for self-government.
• It bridged the gap between early nationalist phases and the Gandhian era.
Modern History.Revolutionary Nationalism (Advanced):
REVOLUTIONARY NATIONALISM IN INDIA

Introduction
• Revolutionary Nationalism represented the militant strand of the Indian National Movement which sought to overthrow British rule through armed struggle.
• It emerged as a reaction to the failure of moderate constitutional methods and the suppression of extremist politics after 1908.
• The movement was characterized by secret societies, political assassinations, and attempts to incite armed rebellion.

Nature of Revolutionary Nationalism
• Individual heroism and secret conspiracies.
• Urban-based, middle-class youth participation.
• Ideological mix of nationalism, anarchism and socialism (later phase).

PYQ Trap
• Not a mass movement; largely limited to educated youth.

PHASES OF REVOLUTIONARY MOVEMENT

Early Phase (1905–1915)
• Triggered by Partition of Bengal (1905).
• Strong presence in Bengal and Maharashtra.

Features
• Political assassinations.
• Bomb attacks on officials.

Important Organisations

Anushilan Samiti
• Founded in Bengal.
• Focus on physical training and revolutionary activities.

Jugantar Group
• More radical faction in Bengal.
• Involved in bomb-making and assassinations.

Abhinav Bharat
• Founded by V.D. Savarkar.
• Active in Maharashtra and London.

PYQ Trap
• Savarkar → India House + Abhinav Bharat.

IMPORTANT EVENTS

Alipore Bomb Case (1908)
• Attempt to assassinate Magistrate Kingsford.
• Aurobindo Ghosh arrested but later acquitted.

Muzaffarpur Bomb Incident (1908)
• Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki.

PYQ Trap
• Khudiram Bose → youngest revolutionary martyr.

Delhi Conspiracy Case (1912)
• Bomb attack on Viceroy Lord Hardinge.

Ghadar Phase (1913–1917)

Introduction
• Overseas revolutionary movement.

Features
• Attempt to incite armed rebellion in India during World War I.

Leaders
• Lala Hardayal
• Kartar Singh Sarabha

Outcome
• Failed due to lack of coordination and British intelligence.

PYQ Trap
• Ghadar → USA + Canada based.

Revolutionary Activities Abroad

India House (London)
• Founded by Shyamji Krishna Varma.

Important Personalities
• Madan Lal Dhingra (assassinated Curzon Wyllie).

Berlin Committee
• Planned revolt with German support during WWI.

Later Phase (1919–1930)

Introduction
• Shift towards organized revolutionary groups.

Hindustan Republican Association (HRA)
• Founded in 1924.

Kakori Conspiracy (1925)
• Looting of train carrying government money.

Leaders
• Ram Prasad Bismil
• Ashfaqulla Khan

PYQ Trap
• Kakori → HRA, not HSRA.

Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)

Introduction
• Reorganized HRA into HSRA in 1928.

Ideology
• Shift towards socialism.

Leaders
• Bhagat Singh
• Chandrashekhar Azad

Major Events

Lahore Conspiracy Case
• Saunders assassination (1928).

Central Legislative Assembly Bomb Case (1929)
• Non-lethal bombs thrown by Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt.

PYQ Trap
• Bomb thrown to “make the deaf hear” (not to kill).

CHITTAGONG ARMOURY RAID (1930)

Introduction
• Led by Surya Sen.

Features
• Attempt to capture British armoury.

Outcome
• Suppressed after prolonged struggle.

COMMON CHARACTERISTICS

Important Points
• Secret and decentralized operations.
• Youth-driven nationalism.
• Focus on symbolic acts to inspire masses.

Ideological Evolution

Early Phase
• Nationalist + anti-colonial.

Later Phase
• Socialist influence (Bhagat Singh).

Significance

Political Impact
• Created psychological fear among British.
• Inspired youth towards nationalism.

Strategic Impact
• Complemented mass movements indirectly.

Limitations

Important Points
• Lack of mass support.
• Poor coordination among groups.
• Strong British intelligence network.

PYQ Trap
• Failure mainly due to isolation from masses.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Moderates → constitutional agitation.
• Extremists → passive resistance.
• Revolutionaries → armed struggle.

Conclusion
• Revolutionary nationalism added a militant dimension to the freedom struggle.
• Though it failed to overthrow British rule, it played a crucial role in inspiring nationalist consciousness and intensifying resistance.
Modern History.Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22):
NON-COOPERATION MOVEMENT (1920–1922)

Introduction
• The Non-Cooperation Movement was the first large-scale mass movement launched by Mahatma Gandhi against British rule.
• It marked the transition from elite politics to mass-based nationalism.
• The movement aimed to achieve Swaraj through peaceful and non-violent means by withdrawing cooperation from British institutions.

Background
• Rowlatt Act (1919) – repressive legislation allowing detention without trial.
• Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919) – brutal killing of civilians in Amritsar.
• Khilafat Movement – demand to protect Ottoman Caliphate.
• Economic hardships after World War I.

PYQ Trap
• NCM was linked with both Punjab wrongs and Khilafat issue.

Objectives

Important Points
• Attainment of Swaraj.
• Boycott of British institutions.
• Promotion of national unity.

Methods

Negative Programme
• Boycott of legislative councils.
• Boycott of government schools and colleges.
• Boycott of law courts.
• Boycott of foreign goods.
• Surrender of titles and honours.

Positive Programme
• Promotion of Swadeshi and Khadi.
• Establishment of national educational institutions.
• Promotion of Hindu-Muslim unity.

PYQ Trap
• Movement had both boycott (negative) and constructive (positive) programmes.

Spread of Movement

Important Points
• Urban participation – students, lawyers, middle class.
• Rural participation – peasants in Awadh, Bihar, Andhra.
• Tribal participation – forest satyagrahas.

Regional Movements
• Awadh – Baba Ramchandra led peasant movement.
• Andhra – Chirala-Perala movement.
• Kerala – Moplah rebellion (violent dimension).

PYQ Trap
• Moplah rebellion associated with NCM but had communal angle.

Role of Congress

Important Points
• Nagpur Session (1920) reorganized Congress.
• Adoption of non-cooperation programme.

Participation

Important Points
• Massive surrender of titles.
• Boycott of elections.
• Growth of national schools.

Limitations

Political
• Uneven participation across regions.
• Lack of full control over mass actions.

Social
• Emergence of local grievances leading to violence.

Chauri Chaura Incident (1922)

Introduction
• Violent clash in Gorakhpur district.

Event
• Police station burnt and policemen killed.

Impact
• Gandhi withdrew the movement.

PYQ Trap
• NCM withdrawn due to violence at Chauri Chaura (key fact).

Consequences

Political Impact
• Demonstrated strength of mass movement.
• Shifted focus to constructive work.

Organizational Impact
• Strengthened Congress base among masses.

Psychological Impact
• Increased confidence among Indians.

Reasons for Withdrawal

Important Points
• Commitment to non-violence.
• Fear of uncontrolled mass uprising.

PYQ Trap
• Withdrawal due to principle of non-violence, not failure of movement.

Significance

Important Points
• First mass-based nationwide movement.
• Brought peasants, workers and women into politics.
• Undermined legitimacy of British rule.

Comparative Analysis

Important Points
• Swadeshi Movement → urban and limited.
• NCM → mass-based and nationwide.

Conclusion
• The Non-Cooperation Movement marked a decisive turning point in the Indian National Movement.
• It transformed the struggle into a mass movement and laid the foundation for future Gandhian campaigns.
Modern History.Swaraj Party (1923):
SWARAJ PARTY (1923)

Introduction
• The Swaraj Party was formed in 1923 as a response to the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
• It aimed to enter legislative councils to obstruct colonial governance from within.
• It represented a strategic shift within the Indian National Movement.

Background
• Withdrawal of Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922 created political vacuum.
• Debate within Congress on future strategy.
• Split between 'No-Changers' and 'Pro-Changers'.

Formation

Important Personalities
• C.R. Das (President)
• Motilal Nehru

PYQ Trap
• C.R. Das → main architect of Swaraj Party.

Ideology

Features
• Entry into legislative councils.
• Obstruction of British policies from within.
• Use of councils as political platform.

PYQ Trap
• Strategy = “Council Entry” (key concept).

Objectives

Important Points
• Destroy colonial governance through obstruction.
• Expose limitations of constitutional reforms.
• Continue struggle within legal framework.

Methods

Features
• Blocking budgets and bills.
• Opposing government measures.
• Using councils for nationalist propaganda.

PYQ Trap
• Swarajists aimed to “wreck the councils from within”.

Achievements

Important Points
• Won significant seats in elections (1923).
• Successfully obstructed government functioning.
• Raised nationalist issues in legislatures.

Role in Councils

Examples
• Rejection of budget proposals.
• Criticism of colonial administration.

Limitations

Political
• Limited powers of legislative councils.
• British control over executive.

Organizational
• Internal divisions within party.

Decline

Causes
• Death of C.R. Das (1925).
• Withdrawal of support by some leaders.
• Rise of new political strategies.

PYQ Trap
• Decline linked with death of C.R. Das.

Relation with Congress

Important Points
• Remained within Congress framework.
• Represented tactical division, not ideological split.

No-Changers vs Pro-Changers

No-Changers
• Favoured constructive work (Gandhians).

Pro-Changers (Swarajists)
• Favoured council entry.

PYQ Trap
• No-Changers → Gandhi followers.

Significance

Political Impact
• Kept political momentum alive after NCM.
• Demonstrated limits of colonial reforms.

Strategic Impact
• Introduced new form of political struggle.

Comparative Analysis

Important Points
• NCM → boycott of councils.
• Swaraj Party → entry into councils.

Conclusion
• The Swaraj Party played a crucial role in sustaining the nationalist movement during a transitional phase.
• It highlighted both the possibilities and limitations of working within colonial institutions.
Modern History.Simon Commission (1927):
SIMON COMMISSION (1927)

Introduction
• The Simon Commission was appointed by the British Government in 1927 to review the working of the Government of India Act, 1919.
• It was a statutory commission set up ahead of schedule to suggest constitutional reforms in India.

Background
• Government of India Act, 1919 provided for a review after 10 years.
• British government appointed the commission earlier in 1927.

Composition

Important Points
• Headed by Sir John Simon.
• Total 7 members.
• All members were British (no Indian representation).

PYQ Trap
• Simon Commission = All-white commission (key fact).

Reaction in India

Introduction
• Strong opposition across India.

Features
• Boycott by Indian National Congress.
• Protest slogans – “Simon Go Back”.
• Participation of students, lawyers and political groups.

Role of Leaders

Important Personalities
• Lala Lajpat Rai led protests in Lahore.

Incident
• Lathi charge during protest led to his death.

PYQ Trap
• Lala Lajpat Rai died due to protest against Simon Commission.

Support for Commission

Important Points
• Supported by some groups like Muslim League (initially divided).
• Some liberals cooperated with commission.

Outcome

Political Impact
• Strengthened national unity against British rule.
• Increased demand for self-government.

Simon Commission Report (1930)

Important Points
• Recommended abolition of dyarchy in provinces.
• Suggested federal structure.
• No immediate grant of dominion status.

PYQ Trap
• Recommended end of dyarchy at provincial level.

Consequences

Important Developments
• Nehru Report (1928) as Indian response.
• Demand for complete independence gained momentum.

Significance

Political Impact
• Exposed British disregard for Indian opinion.
• Intensified nationalist movement.

Strategic Impact
• Led to formulation of constitutional alternatives by Indians.

Comparative Analysis

Important Points
• 1919 Act → dyarchy introduced.
• Simon Commission → recommended abolition of dyarchy.

Conclusion
• The Simon Commission became a turning point in the Indian National Movement.
• Its exclusion of Indians united diverse political groups and strengthened the demand for self-rule.
Modern History.Lahore Session of INC (1929):
LAHORE SESSION OF INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS (1929)

Introduction
• The Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress was held in December 1929.
• It is one of the most significant sessions in the history of the freedom struggle.
• It marked the formal declaration of ‘Purna Swaraj’ (Complete Independence) as the goal of the national movement.

Background
• Failure of constitutional reforms to satisfy Indian demands.
• Rejection of Dominion Status as insufficient.
• Growing nationalist pressure after Simon Commission and Nehru Report.

President

Important Personality
• Jawaharlal Nehru was elected as the President of the session.

PYQ Trap
• Nehru presided over Lahore Session (1929).

Purna Swaraj Resolution

Introduction
• Declaration of complete independence from British rule.

Features
• Rejection of Dominion Status.
• Assertion of full sovereignty for India.

PYQ Trap
• Lahore Session → Purna Swaraj (key link).

Independence Day Declaration

Important Points
• 26 January 1930 declared as Independence Day.
• Nationwide celebrations organized.

PYQ Trap
• 26 January celebrated as Independence Day before 1950.

Programme of Action

Features
• Call for Civil Disobedience Movement.
• Non-payment of taxes.
• Boycott of British institutions.

Significance

Political Impact
• Clear shift from reform to complete independence.
• Unified nationalist goal.

Strategic Impact
• Prepared ground for Civil Disobedience Movement.

Symbolic Importance
• Tricolour flag hoisted on the banks of Ravi river.

PYQ Trap
• Flag hoisting at Ravi river associated with Lahore Session.

Consequences

Important Points
• Launch of Civil Disobedience Movement (1930).
• Strengthening of mass nationalism.

Comparative Analysis

Important Points
• Lucknow Session (1916) → Hindu-Muslim unity.
• Lahore Session (1929) → Purna Swaraj declaration.

Conclusion
• The Lahore Session marked a decisive turning point in the Indian National Movement.
• It transformed the demand from constitutional reforms to complete independence and intensified the struggle against British rule.
Modern History.Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34):
CIVIL DISOBEDIENCE MOVEMENT (1930–1934)

Introduction
• The Civil Disobedience Movement was a major phase of the Indian National Movement led by Mahatma Gandhi.
• It aimed at breaking unjust colonial laws and asserting the right to self-rule.
• It followed the Lahore Session (1929) which declared Purna Swaraj as the objective.

Background
• Failure of constitutional reforms and dissatisfaction with British policies.
• Simon Commission boycott and Nehru Report developments.
• Declaration of Purna Swaraj in 1929.

PYQ Trap
• Civil Disobedience directly linked with Purna Swaraj resolution.

Objectives

Important Points
• Attainment of complete independence.
• Protest against unjust colonial laws.
• Mobilization of masses.

Methods

Features
• Violation of laws (especially salt laws).
• Non-payment of taxes.
• Boycott of foreign goods.
• Resignation from government services.

PYQ Trap
• CDM = active law breaking (unlike NCM which was passive boycott).

DANDI MARCH (1930)

Introduction
• Starting point of Civil Disobedience Movement.

Event
• Gandhi marched from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi.
• Broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

Significance
• Symbolic challenge to British authority.
• Mobilized masses across India.

PYQ Trap
• Dandi March = Salt Satyagraha (core prelim fact).

SPREAD OF MOVEMENT

Important Points
• Participation of peasants, women, students and workers.
